sent_emails.subject: Re: AgriProve - A soil carbon conversation worth having
sent_emails.body: Hi Scott, Sorry we keep missing each other on the phone. I wanted to follow up and share a little more about what a soil carbon project actually means on the ground — because it's rarely just about the credits. Carbon is a signal. When it rises in your soil, it tells you something real is changing — water is being held longer, microbial life is recovering, nutrients are cycling more efficiently. Pasture responds better. Carrying capacity improves. The land starts doing more of the work. These aren't side effects of a carbon project — they're the reason the most experienced farmers we work with tell us the practice change was worth it regardless of the credit income. The credit is how we measure and reward that progress. Through our HORIZON platform, that measurement happens annually — meaning you're not waiting five years to see a return. You're tracking your soil, earning on your improvement, and building a clearer picture of how your country is performing over time. Productivity. Profitability. Long-term resilience. In our experience, when carbon is managed well, all three tend to move together. I'd genuinely enjoy walking you through what this could look like on your property. When would suit? sent_emails.subject: Re: AgriProve - A soil carbon conversation worth having
sent_emails.body: Hi Norman, I wanted to follow up and see if you can provide the lot and plan numbers and I will be able to genrate a freesoil carbon report known as a HORIZON snapshot for you this week. Happy to answer any questions or jump on a call when the timing suits. to share a little more about what a soil carbon project actually means on the ground — because it's rarely just about the credits. Carbon is a signal. When it rises in your soil, it tells you something real is changing — water is being held longer, microbial life is recovering, nutrients are cycling more efficiently. Pasture responds better. Carrying capacity improves. The land starts doing more of the work. These aren't side effects of a carbon project — they're the reason the most experienced farmers we work with tell us the practice change was worth it regardless of the credit income. The credit is how we measure and reward that progress. Through our HORIZON platform, that measurement happens annually — meaning you're not waiting five years to see a return. You're tracking your soil, earning on your improvement, and building a clearer picture of how your country is performing over time. Productivity. Profitability. Long-term resilience. In our experience, when carbon is managed well, all three tend to move together. I'd genuinely enjoy walking you through what this could look like on your property and I'll follow up with a call this week. sent_emails.body: Hi Jamie, I hope you're well and sorry we keep missing each other on the phone. I wanted to follow up and share a little more about what a soil carbon project actually means on the ground — because it's rarely just about the credits. Carbon is a signal. When it rises in your soil, it tells you something real is changing — water is being held longer, microbial life is recovering, nutrients are cycling more efficiently. Pasture responds better. Carrying capacity improves. The land starts doing more of the work. These aren't side effects of a carbon project — they're the reason the most experienced farmers we work with tell us the practice improvement was worth it regardless of the credit income. We have a specialist grazier on the road with us, Hobbs Magaret, currently visiting producers across the Riverina who are doing interesting things on their country. Better pasture results, smarter grazing, stronger ground cover — the kind of results paid for in early mornings and tough seasons. sent_emails.subject: Follow up for our call this week— the key points
sent_emails.body: Hi Geoff, Thanks again for the call this week. I just wanted to come back to you on the key points you raised over the phone this week. 1. Rainfall and sequestration viability you mentioned that you have been told by others that soil carbon is "wholly and solely reliant on rainfall" and is potentially sceptical about whether drier conditions stack up. Our position is that rainfall is a necessary condition for carbon sequestration, but it does not cause carbon sequestration. We have seen projects with high rainfall that have not resulted in sequestration and have seen low rainfall projects be awarded credits. It is our belief and observations from our portfolio that management, that is how you capture, use and manage the water on your land is a critical aspect to carbon sequestration. 2. Carbon credits and carbon neutrality claims You have heard at a meeting (possibly a Riverina co-op event) that selling ACCUs means losing carbon neutrality status, and that one farmer had to buy credits back at a premium to restore their neutral balance. This is not necessarily true. A claim of carbon neutrality can be made when the emissions from a property are neutralised via sequestration or offsets. Claiming carbon neutrality and participating in a carbon project are two independent programs. Each requires their own audits and assessments if a verifiable claim is to be made. In determining whether a business is carbon neutral, all emissions sources are accounted for (e.g. livestock, fertiliser, lime, fuel, electricity, etc) and then checked against any sequestration (trees and soil). If there is a deficit, where total emissions exceed total sequestration, then to claim carbon neutrality you must source an eligible offsets unit and retire that unit to be able to claim carbon neutrality (i.e. offsetting emissions). An ACCU is one of a number of eligible offsets units, so it can be ‘retired’ to support this claim. If there is a surplus of sequestration, (i.e. carbon stores from trees or soil is greater than emissions) then there is no need to purchase offsets to claim carbon neutrality. Additionally, in this scenario, any credits that have been generated above that carbon neutral amount, can be sold, and the claim can still be made that you are carbon neutral. Where this messaging in industry becomes murky is that if you sell all ACCUs (that have been generated via soil or tree sequestration) then this sequestration cannot be measured against the emissions to claim carbon neutrality. The claim that you can’t sell ACCUs and claim carbon neutrality is based on the assumption that sequestration will not exceed emissions and there will be no surplus ACCUs to be able to sell. This is not correct. The key determinant in claiming carbon neutrality is that the emissions have been neutralised either via sequestration and/or offsets. If you generate ACCUs through participating in a soil carbon or ACCU scheme project and hold them in your ANREU account, you have the flexibility to sell, retain/hold or retire the ACCUs depending on your needs and priorities, and the yearly carbon emissions assessment. If you do not have an ANREU account, you cannot hold ACCUs to offset against your emissions, you must source these eligible credits units by purchasing on a secondary market. In partnering with AgriProve and participating in a soil carbon project, you will be set up with your own ANREU account, and that 75% of the ACCUs awarded to the project will be held in your own ANREU account to use in the manner that you have deemed best for your business. 3. ACCU pricing and the "premium" question You'd heard $68/ACCU on ABC News and was trying to make sense of it against spot ($37.50 at call time). You're across the basic answer now (broker-facilitated premiums for high-integrity credits with a good story), but it's natural to be thinking hard about whether the economics stack up and what his exit options look like at different price points. sent_emails.subject: Restrictions realting to irrigation for your carbon projects:
sent_emails.body: Hi Jason, Thanks again for today. A summary of the issues relating to irrigation for your carbon projects: Irrigation is a restricted activity under s.12(8) of the Methodology After completion of the baseline sampling round, irrigation may be applied to CEAs (Carbon Estimation Areas) within a project area only if both of the following apply: disregarding new irrigation, the annual level of irrigation for the project area is not more than 20% greater than the highest annual level of irrigation in the baseline period; disregarding new irrigation, the 5-yearly total level of irrigation for the project area is not more than 20% greater than the total level of irrigation in the baseline period. For example, if there was 10ML of irrigation applied in 2020, 5ML of irrigation in 2021 and none during the other baseline years, the project/CEA is restricted to: Using no more than 12ML of irrigation in any 1 year, and Using no more than 18ML in a 5-year period. 'New irrigation' is defined as “new or additional irrigation applied to land in a project area using water obtained through irrigation efficiency savings made after the date on which the section 27 declaration of the project was made” and is a result of improving the efficiency of irrigated water through one or both of the following: (i) on-farm irrigation infrastructure located within the project area; (ii) management practices within the project area This means that ‘new irrigation’ is essentially a redistribution of irrigation derived from efficiency savings, not simply applying more water. There is no restriction on how the water is redistributed, for example to other parts of the CEA under new irrigation infrastructure, so long as the water is derived from those efficiency savings. Hope that adresses your question and let me know if you have any others. sent_emails.subject: Following up on our conversation yesterday
sent_emails.body: HI Brian, Thanks for your time on the phone yesterday, I want to ensure that I can provide the clarity and transparency you raised in our call. The use of "may" in the agreement is there to provide flexibility to adapt internal process or actions as the project develops in practice, rather than committing to a process that may not suit the conditions on the ground. It is not there to show a lack of commitment or be uncertain for what we deliver. It also reflects something that is true of soil carbon broadly: we cannot provide guarantee on what any project will return, and we won't claim that we can. What the agreement does commit to unconditionally are the services we deliver: All soil sampling after baseline (you only pay for the initial baseline sampling) Project design and onboarding Soil results analysis and presentation, including all Method calculations Registration, monitoring, reporting and audit management ACCU issuance and distribution to you If there are specific clauses that still read as uncommitted, please flag them and we'll walk through each one directly. This is a shared model. Your risk is the upfront cost of baseline sampling, and the commitment to make improvements to your farming operation for soil carbon purposes — with no guarantee those activities will produce ACCUs that offset that cost. From that point, the risk sits with AgriProve. We operate on a success fee — if no credits are generated, we don't get paid. All costs, both time and financial, for reporting, sampling coordination, project design, monitoring and measurement across the first five-year period are borne by us. We also manage the relationship with the Clean Energy Regulator, including the responsibility to relinquish credits if requested. The only circumstance in which that obligation can be passed back to you is if you have materially breached the agreement. This carries through for the life of the project, whereby we will commit to completing the work and if there are no ACCUs we do not get paid. The 25-year term is a requirement of the ACCU scheme — it applies to every registered project, not just AgriProve's. There are genuine exit points along the way. Prior to ACCUs being awarded to your project, you can elect to discontinue at any time and for any reason. If you exit within that five-year window, the only cost is that the baseline sampling cannot be recovered through the scheme. There is no further obligation to AgriProve or the Clean Energy Regulator. We provide annual reports and assessments leading into the five-year review so there are no surprises — you'll have a clear picture of whether your project is tracking well before that decision point arrives. There are additional options once ACCUs have been issued, that we can walk through should this be of concern. Lastly, Government concerns. This is a fair and legitimate concern. The straightforward answer is that no one can guarantee what any government does over a 25-year period. What we can tell you is that a registered soil carbon project sits inside a legal framework that creates real barriers to retrospective change. Your project, once registered, is a legally binding contract with the Clean Energy Regulator and Australian Government. Any material change to the scheme would carry significant legal and financial implications for the government, which is why historically, changes to the ACCU scheme have applied to projects registered going forward, not to projects already registered. Our agreement also contains force majeure provisions that apply in the event of a material change to the relevant law, meaning if the scheme were changed in a way that fundamentally affected your project, there are provisions to exit the project. Beyond the legal framework, the ACCU scheme now has substantial institutional and corporate investment behind it. sent_emails.body: Hi George, It was great reconnecting with you yesterday about Castle Hill. I've put together your HORIZON Snapshot, which gives you a detailed picture of what your property looks like from a soil carbon perspective. It's attached to this email and click the link here to view also.: https://canva.link/gn7iigz2t8893k4 The short version: Castle Hill has strong fundamentals. That is a substantial carbon asset, built on the grazing operation you are already running. Your Vertosol country in particular is well suited to this. Vertosols carry high water holding capacity, high productivity, and high carbon stability, making them one of the best soil types for long-term carbon accumulation under the ERF. Combined with your Chromosol country and 640mm of annual rainfall, the conditions at Castle Hill are genuinely well positioned for a project of this scale. The HORIZON Snapshot attached covers your HORIZON zone map, soil indicators, and two pricing options. sent_emails.subject: RE: KML of grazing areas
sent_emails.body: Hi Ben, You may have misinterpreted that one, but your concern is tottally understandable. Essentially, you can’t run a soil carbon project on a given area of land and convert that same land to environmental plantings for separate carbon credits. But you’re not locked out of environmental planting as a future avenue on different parts of their property, and the soil carbon project doesn't extinguish that optionality elsewhere on the farm. If there's any ambiguity about the eligibility of your specific land against the forest potential criteria, that's something I would flag with the project setup team to assess during the mapping and stratification process before registration. We would then get the soil carbon project mapped around the area you intended for environmental plantings and have the flexibility to move boundaries of the mapped project over the lifespan of the project. Hope this answers the question. Also, below is a brief that I have been working on with another sugarcane farm. I have applied XXXX for privacy of the client (I hope you don’t mind) that I’m also working on a project with. I thought this would be helpful for you to see. The Concept XXX farming system is built around a ~5-year cane rotation, with paddocks spending 12–18 months in fallow between cane crops. Rather than leaving fallow ground bare or under conventional management, XXXX returns those paddocks to multi-species pasture under high-density grazing, managed using E Shepherd (virtual fencing technology). The explicit goal of the pasture/fallow phase is to rebuild soil carbon before the paddock returns to cane production. Over a 25-year project period this would yield approximately 5 pasture rotations. His broader aims include: * Reducing reliance on synthetic inputs (fertiliser, chemicals) by rebuilding soil biology through the pasture phase * Incorporating robotics into the cane production phase for more precise input application * Using biodiversity monitoring robots to quantify ecosystem improvements alongside carbon * Proving the model on his own farm first, then rolling it out regionally with the data to back it up The expected carbon trajectory was discussed: carbon will increase during grazing/fallow phases and decline slightly during cropping phases, but the overall 25-year trajectory should be net positive — a "ladder" pattern where the incline outpaces the decline over time. ________________________________ Strategic Fit XXX has a strong interest in the platform play, data integration, and the suite of metrics AgriProve is building toward. This makes him not just a project opportunity but a potential proof-of-concept and regional advocate, given his connections across >5,000ha of regional cane. The opportunity is relatively small in isolation (XXXXha grazing component), but the bigger picture value lies in: * Proving the model works in a cane rotation system * Generating data that could underpin regional rollout * George's regional influence and connectivity as a pathway to scale ________________________________ Project Mechanics The registration and crediting structure needs careful sequencing given the rotation cycle: 1. Register the project while paddocks are still under cane — ideally just before the final harvest prior to entering fallow 2. Declare the project under cane so the declaration date is established 3. Baseline immediately upon entering fallow — so ACCU accumulation begins as soon as the carbon trajectory starts moving 4. Roll through each rotation — approximately every 5 years — repeating the process across the project life The key risk flagged by Will: don't baseline and then wait for fallow to begin, as you lose the benefit of capturing the full carbon increase from the start of the pasture phase. Timing the declaration right before the last cane harvest is the optimal approach. ________________________________ Next Steps A follow-up call has been scheduled for Friday April 10, The focus will be on: * Project mechanics…

sent_emails.subject: Re: KML of grazing areas
sent_emails.body: Hi Ben, Thank you for your patience while we worked through the detailed exclusion mapping for the Bundaberg Sugar portfolio. I am pleased to share your new HORIZON Snapshot, which now reflects the grazing-specific eligible areas across your four properties spanning the Burnett River corridor, coastal hinterland, and estuarine flats north and west of Bundaberg. Click to view link to the report also.: https://canva.link/uiu7nw2pywdh7gi Here is what the analysis shows: Your combined grazing-eligible area is 1,187.90 hectares across three estimated soil carbon projects, with an estimated potential of around 148,488 ACCUs over a 25-year crediting period. That is a meaningful long-term carbon asset built directly over the grazing management you are already running on this country. Your portfolio sits within the 1,001–1,100mm annual rainfall band, one of the strongest performance categories in the ERF framework. Soils across the portfolio are predominantly Sodosol, which responds well to gypsum application, one of the eligible management activities under the ERF soil carbon method. This gives your grazing country a clear and practical lever to build carbon performance over the project term. Approximately 60% of your eligible area is at optimal soil depth of greater than one metre, and pH across the portfolio ranges from 4.66 to 5.74, consistent with mildly to moderately acidic profiles that also open the door to lime application as an additional eligible activity. Two confirmed AgriProve projects are operating within 20 kilometres of the Bundaberg Sugar properties, which gives us confidence that this climate zone supports measurable carbon outcomes. On the economics, the baseline investment is straightforward at this scale: Option 1 involves a baseline sampling cost of $22,680 ex GST, with AgriProve's 25% success fee covering all ongoing project administration, sampling, auditing, and reporting across the project lifetime. Option 2 allows you to defer the full $22,680 baseline cost to be repaid from ACCUs generated within the first five years at $12.50 per ACCU, equivalent to 1,814 ACCUs. There is no upfront balance required under this option, with the 25% success fee applying as above. We take care of the complexity from here: sampling design, baseline field work (our team comes to you), laboratory analysis, ERF registration, ongoing reporting to the Clean Energy Regulator, subsequent sampling every five years, audit coordination, and ACCU issuance. Your role is providing property access and continuing the grazing management you are already doing. I would love to find a time to walk you through the snapshot and answer any questions. Would you be available for a call this week or next? sent_emails.body: Hi Ben, Thanks for taking the time to connect and sorry we missed each other yesterday. I've put together your HORIZON Snapshot for Muskerry, and I wanted to walk you through what we're seeing across your property. See attached in this email and provided here in a clickable link to view.: https://canva.link/2b3s7iftu46fpjg Your eligible area comes in at 810 hectares, representing 87.6% of your total property across the three parcels. That's a strong result, and the soil profile here gives us some genuinely interesting things to work with. The HORIZON model is estimating a potential of approximately 50,600 ACCUs over 25 years at a rate of 2.5 credits per hectare per year, based on your 506 mm average annual rainfall and grazing enterprise. At current market conditions, that represents a meaningful long-term carbon asset layered over your existing land management. A couple of things worth highlighting from the analysis: Your soils are mapped entirely as Sodosol, a soil type that responds well to targeted management. The pH reading of 5.12 to 5.67 across the eligible area is a particularly relevant finding. Both lime application for acid soil remediation and gypsum treatment for sodium management are eligible activities under the Emissions Reduction Fund. These aren't things you need to do to register a project, but if they're already part of your management thinking, they directly support the carbon outcome we're building toward. Your depth profile is also strong. Soils across the eligible area range from 0.77 to 2.10 metres, with the majority sitting at optimal depth for carbon accumulation. In terms of next steps, the attached Snapshot steps through the full analysis including the project economics. I'd welcome the chance to talk through what this looks like for your operation. Let me know if you have any questions on the HORIZON Snapshot, and when could we set up a time to discuss further? sent_emails.subject: Re: AgriProve - Introduction
sent_emails.body: Hi Tom, I hope you've been keeping well. I wanted to follow up and share a little more about what a soil carbon project actually means on the ground — because it's rarely just about the credits. Carbon is a signal. When it rises in your soil, it tells you something real is changing — water is being held longer, microbial life is recovering, nutrients are cycling more efficiently. Pasture responds better. Carrying capacity improves. The land starts doing more of the work. These aren't side effects of a carbon project — they're the reason the most experienced farmers we work with tell us the practice change or implementing slight tweaks to existing practice was worth it regardless of the credit income. Productivity. profitability and long-term resilience. In our experience, when carbon is managed well, all three tend to move together. I'd genuinely enjoy walking you through what this could look like on your property. Our Ag researcher from who’s based in Albury for a few months is grazier himself, written books on grazing management, and he’s been visiting operations across the Riverina. sent_emails.subject: AgriProve -& Tags for Tonnes Enquiry
sent_emails.body: Hi Nick, Thanks for reaching out — great to hear you're across both sides of this, because that's exactly where the value sits. Here's the plain version of what we're offering. On the ag-tech side, AgriProve has partnered with two of Australia's leading livestock monitoring platforms — Ceres Tag and mOOvement. Both deliver real-time GPS tracking and grazing behaviour data that flows directly into our Ready Graze platform. Ceres Tag Ranch devices are solar-powered and satellite-enabled with no Wi-Fi or towers required. mOOvement tags are lightweight and well suited to operations already running a connected herd management system. We can work out which fits your setup best on a call. On the soil carbon side, AgriProve has registered 76% of all soil carbon projects under the Clean Energy Regulator's ACCU Scheme. A project with us means your land is sampled, a baseline established, and as your soil organic carbon builds, you generate ACCUs — credits that are sold for real income. Improved grazing management is one of the primary levers for building that carbon. The connection between the two is what makes this compelling: the grazing data your tags generate supports the land management reporting requirements of your soil carbon project. One investment, doing two jobs. Both technologies are available through the AgriProve Marketplace: https://app.agriprove.io/marketplace at app.agriprove.io/marketplace — where you can access them using cash, existing ACCUs, or future ACCUs generated through your project. No upfront cost required. Best place to start is a HORIZON Snapshot — a no-obligation property analysis that maps your carbon opportunity before you commit to anything. Happy to run through it on a call. Are you free this week? sent_emails.subject: Re: Fwd: AgriProve - Farm Visit with Hobbs Margaret
sent_emails.body: Hi Jon, Not a problem at all, great questions. See responses below: 1. What happens if carbon measurements decrease after ACCUs have been sold? This is about what the industry calls a "reversal" — where soil carbon levels drop below what was previously measured and credited. Under the ACCU Scheme, the Clean Energy Regulator can issue a relinquishment notice requiring ACCUs to be handed back if a reversal is detected. The key protection for landholders here is Clause 7.4 of the Master T&Cs, which states that AgriProve (as Project Proponent) is responsible for complying with any relinquishment notice except where the notice directly results from a breach of the agreement by the Landholder and/or Operator. In plain terms: If carbon levels drop due to normal variation, drought, or circumstances outside the landholder's control, AgriProve wears the relinquishment risk — not the landholder. This is one of the key commercial benefits of AgriProve acting as Project Proponent. If the drop is caused by the landholder breaching the agreement — for example, by undertaking Restricted Activities (Clause 2.4(3) and Attachment C) such as deep tillage or land clearing within the project area — liability can shift back to the landholder. The practical takeaway: as long as the landholder sticks to the Land Management Strategy and avoids Restricted Activities, the relinquishment risk sits with AgriProve. This is an important differentiator worth emphasising with clients. 2. Is the 25% AgriProve fee fixed, or can it move up or down? The short answer is: it can only move in the landholder's favour. The fee is set at 25% as established in the Key Commercial Terms. Under Clause 20.2 of the Master T&Cs, any amendments to the agreement cannot have a material adverse effect on the Landholder or Operator. An increase in AgriProve's fee from 25% would clearly constitute a material adverse effect, so it cannot be applied without written consent from all parties (Clause 20.4). The only automatic adjustment that can occur is downward. Under Clause 20.3, if AgriProve reduces its standard market offer below 25% (for example, to 20%), existing clients are automatically moved to the lower rate on a pro-rata basis from the next anniversary of the Start Date. So early adopters won't be locked into a higher fee if AgriProve's standard offering drops. In summary: the fee can go down if market conditions change, but it cannot go up without the landholder's written agreement. 3. Termination — what are the ramifications for ACCUs already sold? Termination mechanics are covered under Clause 13 of the Master T&Cs, and the implications differ depending on how and why the agreement is terminated. This only applies if the agreement is terminated and the project is revoked (deregistered) with the CER. There are mechanisms for a project to continue without AgriProve, where a project proponent is changed, or project activities are discontinued but the project continues on in an administrative capacity to eliminate the possibility of project deregistration. These are outlined below. If neither of these pathways are taken up, and a project agreement is terminated and the project is deregistered, then the following applies. The critical point is that ACCUs must have been issued to the project. The if a project is deregistered, then there is a regulatory requirement to relinquish ACCUs that have been issued to the project. Here's how it plays out under the main termination scenarios: No reasonable pathway (Clause 13.3): If both parties agree there's no viable path forward (i.e. that despite options presented in Clause 9 or Clause 14 the agreement/project must be terminated), the Operator must transfer back to AgriProve a number of ACCUs equivalent to all Project ACCUs issued to date (both the Operator's 75% and AgriProve's 25% share). sent_emails.body: Hi James, I hope you're well. I'm pleased to share your HORIZON Snapshot for your first property, Weemala. The analysis has identified 58.77 hectares as eligible for a soil carbon project, representing 78.9% of the property. At 1,328 mm of annual rainfall, Weemala sits in our highest ACCU rate band, giving the property an estimated potential of around 8,816 ACCUs over a standard 25-year crediting period. The HORIZON map reveals a strong base of carbon performance across the western and central-western paddocks, with meaningful Opportunity Zones through the eastern and southern areas where targeted grazing management could lift performance further. There is also a notable soil health story at Weemala. The pH data shows strongly acidic conditions across the full eligible area (4.53 to 4.76), and lime application and acid soil remediation are both eligible activities under the ERF. This opens a practical conversation about layering soil health improvement alongside the carbon project, with the costs of those activities potentially supported through the program. As mentioned in our previous conversations, at 58.77 eligible hectares, Weemala sits below the standalone project registration threshold under the ERF. Combined eligible area across your other properties brings the project to the required scale, and Weemala's high-rainfall, high-rate contribution becomes a meaningful part of a larger, commercially viable whole. sent_emails.subject: Some common objections and responses that will help you
sent_emails.body: Hi Shelley, I just wanted to provide you with some common objections and responses you maty encountered with Kevin as a starting point. "I heard of a bloke who ended up owing money back on his carbon project." What they mean: Someone I trust told me this went badly for a farmer, and I don't want to be next. Response: That story almost always traces back to one of two things: either the project was run without a proponent — meaning the farmer was personally on the hook to the regulator — or the project was voluntarily wound up entirely. Neither of those things happen in an AgriProve project, and here's why. As Project Proponent, AgriProve carries the regulatory risk. If carbon stocks decline due to a bad season, measurement variability, or anything outside your control, that's our problem to manage — not yours. You don't receive a bill. You don't return credits. The obligation sits with us, not you. The only scenario where liability could shift back to you is if you deliberately breached the agreement — for example, clearing the project area or converting the land out of an agricultural system. Normal farming, including tough years, doesn't come close to that threshold. On property sale specifically — and this is where most of the scary stories originate — if a farmer ran a project without a proponent and sold the property to someone who didn't want to continue it, they were personally required to return every credit ever generated back to the regulator. That's the debt people have heard about. With AgriProve as proponent, that obligation transfers to us. It's our job to novate the agreement to the incoming landholder. And it's genuinely attractive for an incoming buyer to take on — the baseline has already been paid for, all future sampling and compliance costs are covered by us, and they're inheriting a proven income stream with no setup cost. There's also a five-year project review built in. On the anniversary of your project declaration, we assess performance together. If no carbon increases have occurred and the project isn't working for your country, you have the right to delist at no cost and with no obligations. You're not locked into a failing project. The only situation where you'd ever need to transfer credits back to AgriProve is if both parties agreed there was no viable path forward and the project needed to be fully terminated — and even then, that's our mechanism for managing our regulatory obligation, not a penalty imposed on you. "It's a scam. It's all just greenwashing." What they mean: I've been burned by schemes before and I don't trust anything with a government smell. Response:: That's the most common place people start. And honestly, it's a fair instinct — there have been poorly designed carbon schemes in the past. But this one is built differently. Every tonne of carbon has to be physically measured in your soil, verified by an independent auditor, and approved by the Clean Energy Regulator before a single credit is issued. You don't earn anything we can't prove. If the carbon isn't there, neither is the payment. Closing line: "Scams don't require us to come out and drill cores in your paddocks. The numbers either show up, or they don't — and you only get paid when they do." "I don't trust the government." What they mean: I don't want bureaucrats making decisions about my land. Response: Neither do we. The government doesn't run this project — we do. Your contract is with AgriProve, not a regulator. The Clean Energy Regulator is simply the body that issues the credits and audits the numbers, the same way the ATO processes a tax return. They're in the background. We're the ones on the ground with you for 25 years. Closing line: "You're not entering a compliance program. You're entering a revenue program — with us, not Canberra." sent_emails.subject: Wanted to make sure you heard this from me first
sent_emails.body: Hi Michelle, I hope you are keeping well. I wanted to give you a heads up on a couple of things happening on our end before they land. From 1 July, we're moving to a new mandatory baseline sampling configuration — 24 cores per Carbon Estimation Area, up from the current 12. This comes out of recent independent review work and improves project accuracy and reduces variance, so it's a sound change. But it does affect cost. At current per-core pricing, the difference looks like this: Current configuration (12 cores): ~$8,500 per CEA New configuration from 1 July (24 cores): ~$10,700 per CEA For anyone who has signed their Key Commercial Terms before 30 June, current pricing applies to their baselining. The second thing worth flagging — if your property is in Queensland particularly the central-western region, our sampling crew will be on the ground in May and June. If we can tie your baselining into that window, we can lock in a guaranteed date. After that, we genuinely can't say when we'll next be back in the region — it could be 12 months away, which would potentially push your first crediting cycle out accordingly. I'm not trying to rush your thinking, but I'd rather you have the full picture now than find out later. Happy to run through what it means for your specific property if that's useful — just let me know a time that suits. The analysis covers both properties and identifies approximately 360 hectares of eligible area across the properties, representing 63% of your total land. HORIZON has mapped how carbon is currently distributed across your landscape, giving us a clear picture of where your stronger country sits and where the most significant opportunity lies. A few things worth highlighting from the analysis: Your southern property shows genuine Strength Zone presence through its central and eastern sections, indicating carbon levels above your property median. This is encouraging. The northern property is dominated by Opportunity Zones, which reflects where targeted grazing management has the most capacity to lift carbon performance over time. Your soils are Dermosol and Sodosol across the eligible area, with a rainfall average of 725mm. At an estimated rate of 3.5 ACCUs per hectare per year, the property has a projected potential of approximately 31,479 ACCUs over a 25-year crediting period. Baseline sampling is estimated at $7,984 ex GST, with the option to defer that cost entirely against future ACCUs if preferred. One thing I want to be upfront with you about: at 360 eligible hectares, the property sits just slightly below the 400 hectare threshold for standalone project registration under the ERF. This means participation would be via AgriProve's aggregation pathway, where we group eligible properties together to meet registration requirements. It's a well-established route, and many of our clients across Victoria participate this way. It doesn't change the ACCU potential or the economics for you as a landholder. sent_emails.subject: Your HORIZON Snapshot — Bundaberg Sugar
sent_emails.body: Hi Ben, Thank you for the opportunity to assess the Bundaberg Sugar portfolio. I am pleased to share your HORIZON Snapshot, which covers the four eligible areas spanning the Burnett River corridor and coastal hinterland west and south of Bundaberg. See attached HORIZON Snapshot Report within this email and a click to view link provided here: https://www.canva.com/design/DAHEuM99fNU/6OcIF9EQ7iF8UsIp1mC0HA/watch?utm_content=DAHEuM99fNU&utm_campaign=designshare&utm_medium=link2&utm_source=uniquelinks&utlId=h02e1f5840b Here is what the analysis shows across your grazing country: Approximately 4,770 hectares of your portfolio is estimated as grazing-eligible for a soil carbon project under the Emissions Reduction Fund. Across that area, HORIZON has identified 12 potential projects with an estimated potential of around 596,250 ACCUs over a 25-year crediting period. That is a significant long-term asset layered directly over the grazing management you are already running. Your portfolio sits within the 1,001–1,100mm annual rainfall band, one of the strongest performance categories in the ERF framework, and your soils include Kandosol and Dermosol, which offer good water holding capacity and moderate to moderate-high carbon stability. The depth profile across the portfolio is particularly encouraging, with approximately 65% of your eligible area estimated at optimal depth of greater than one metre. Two confirmed AgriProve projects are operating within 20 kilometres of your eligible project area, which gives us confidence that this climate zone and management context supports measurable carbon outcomes. We take care of the complexity from here: sampling design, baseline field work (our team comes to you), laboratory analysis, ERF registration, ongoing reporting to the Clean Energy Regulator, subsequent sampling every five years, audit coordination, and ACCU issuance. Your role is providing property access and continuing the grazing management you are already doing. It is worth noting that the detailed boundary mapping between your grazing and sugar cane areas will be worked through by our operations team as part of the project design process, so the eligible area figures will be refined further at that stage. I would love to find a time to walk you through the snapshot and answer any questions. Would you be available for a call this week or next? Looking forward to partnering with you on this. sent_emails.body: Hi Shelley, Great speaking with you today — it's exciting to see Plumthorpe Pastoral moving toward intent to project registration. Ahead of our Land Management Strategy Call, I want to make sure we use the time well. There are three things that will help us hit the ground running: Paddock maps for each property — digital files are ideal, but hand-drawn maps showing clear boundary lines work just as well. These let us accurately configure your project areas before the call. Five-year farm management history: https://ap1.hubs.ly/y0Hy120— this is one of the most important pieces of the puzzle. To accurately model your soil carbon baseline and project what your land can sequester, we need a clear picture of how your properties have been managed over the past five years. Think stocking rates, pasture management, any significant land use changes — the more detail the better. Don't worry if it's not perfectly documented; we'll work through it together on the call. The AgriProve Project Proposal (Farm Management): https://ap1.hubs.ly/y0Hy130— I've attached this document and linked it above. It's the foundation of our conversation, so the more detail you can fill in beforehand, the more productive our session will be. If you run into any questions while working through it, just send them through. Our Land Management Strategy Call runs around 45 minutes. The report we prepared for [Property Name] is tailored specifically to your landscape — it's not a generic assessment. What we're hoping to understand at this stage is whether you'd like to take the next step toward project development. We have now completed the HORIZON analysis across Kland Holdings and the numbers are worth paying attention to (see attached in this email or click here to view: https://www.canva.com/design/DAHED03d650/h3-25SBB9DyjS3AKuuXB_g/watch?utm_content=DAHED03d650&utm_campaign=designshare&utm_medium=link2&utm_source=uniquelinks&utlId=h153685c779) Here is what you are sitting on: Across 2,309 eligible hectares, Kland Holdings has an estimated 25-year ACCU potential of approximately 144,000 carbon credits. That is built on your existing grazing operation, on country you already manage, across 6 project areas of roughly 400 hectares each. The southern Riverina corridor is proven ground for AgriProve, with credited projects active in the surrounding region confirming this rainfall band and land type delivers real carbon outcomes. There is also something specific to your farming enterprise worth highlighting. Your HORIZON data shows consistent soil pH readings between 4.71 and 4.97 across the entire eligible area. That is a strongly acidic profile, and under the Emissions Reduction Fund soil carbon method, acid soil remediation through lime application is a recognized eligible activity. That means the pH story here is not a constraint. It is potentially an additional lever for carbon performance on top of grazing management. Why this works: AgriProve has registered soil carbon projects across southern NSW and the broader Riverina region. Active and credited projects in your corridor demonstrate that this climatic zone and soil type, managed well, generates measurable carbon gains and verified ACCUs. Your HORIZON Opportunity Zone coverage across the northern paddocks of both blocks tells us there is genuine room to move performance upward from the current baseline. What we handle: We take care of the complexity: sampling design, baseline field work (our team comes to you), laboratory analysis, ERF registration, ongoing reporting to the Clean Energy Regulator, subsequent sampling every 5 years, audit coordination, and ACCU issuance. Your role is providing property access and continuing the land management you are already doing. That is it. The next step is a 45-minute call to confirm the project design and lock in your sampling slot. I have availability this Thursday or Friday afternoon. Does one of those work for you? Looking forward to partnering with you on this. sent_emails.subject: RE: Your AgriProve HORIZON Snapshot – Apels Road - Land and Expand Opportunity
sent_emails.body: Hi Michelle. As far as the soil organic carbon method is set up, the rules on eligibility are: * Timber country can't be cleared within 7-years of the project registration date (future) or 5-years if new owners. * Vegetation management is allowed, but it must be shown to be a BAU approach. * Clearing/Thinning is relative to the definition of Forest which is 20% canopy cover, over 2m tall and greater in area than 0.2 of a hectare so, we just would need to have additional details regarding it. * Timbered country is eligible, providing that it can be grazed, and sampled, and is not a designated forest. Generally speaking, we'd need more detail on the actual land use and what's required to be cleared as every property has it’s own nuance. sent_emails.subject: Your AgriProve HORIZON Snapshot – Apels Road - Land and Expand Opportunity
sent_emails.body: Hi Michelle, Thanks for your continued interest in exploring soil carbon and the potential of the Apels Road property. I've attached your HORIZON Snapshot, which gives you a clear picture of what the property looks like through our analysis. You have 218.91 eligible hectares across the property, with Kurosol soils dominating 96.5% of the eligible area. Kurosols offer moderate water holding and carbon stability characteristics, and with 725mm of annual rainfall, there's genuine capacity for carbon accumulation under improved management. The analysis shows the eligible area sitting predominantly within Opportunity Zones — with the northern river frontage paddock standing out as the area with the deepest soils (reaching close to 1 metre) and the strongest conditions for carbon building. The eligible area shown is derived from automated satellite analysis and should be treated as a reference. Should circumstances change, our geospatial team conducts a detailed assessment and works with you to capture all managed land appropriately. At 218.91 eligible hectares, this sits below our typical 400ha threshold where project economics work well for landholders. The baseline sampling and ongoing project costs simply don't align with the estimated carbon revenue at this scale, so we're unable to proceed with a registered soil carbon project at this stage. That said, the HORIZON Snapshot gives you a useful picture of where to focus management attention to build soil organic carbon for other valuable outcomes. Directing management focus toward the Opportunity Zones — particularly in the northern paddock and across the central blocks — could support improvements in productivity, water holding capacity, and overall soil health, even without formal carbon crediting. I know this isn't the outcome you were hoping for regarding credits, and we're genuinely disappointed too — Apels Road has favorable rainfall and the Kurosol soils show real potential. At 218.91 eligible hectares, this usually falls below our 400ha project threshold, though with the registration of Boyne Crossing, we would ensure Apels Rd, Toondara would be viable as a registered soil carbon project also. sent_emails.subject: Your AgriProve HORIZON Snapshot – S and G Duncan
sent_emails.body: Hi Steven, Thanks for your interest in exploring soil carbon at your Bullcamp property. I've attached your HORIZON Snapshot, which shows the estimated opportunity based on our analysis across both of your land parcels. You have 233 eligible hectares, with Sodosol soils that — under your 844mm annual rainfall — create conditions suited to carbon accumulation. The analysis shows Strength Zones through the central and southern sections of the western paddocks and across the middle of the northeastern block, where modelled carbon levels currently sit above the property median. Opportunity Zones across the northern and western portions of both parcels indicate where management adjustments could support meaningful gains. With soil depths reaching 1.70m, there's solid capacity for carbon storage in the profile. We're projecting approximately 23,329 ACCUs over 25 years based on your rainfall band — a genuine volume for a property of this scale. The eligible area shown is derived from automated satellite analysis and should be treated as a reference. Our geospatial team conducts a detailed property assessment as part of the next stage, combining expert interpretation with your on-ground knowledge. If you notice managed land that appears to have been excluded, our team will work together with you to review and, where appropriate, include it in your project area. There is one important consideration to share openly: our registered projects are typically structured around a minimum of 400 eligible hectares, where the economics work most effectively for landholders. At 233 ha, your property would need to be paired with a neighbouring property to form a viable registered project. This is a well-travelled path — aggregated projects are common in the South Burnett region — and it's something I'd love to explore with you if you have neighbours who might be interested. In the meantime, the HORIZON analysis gives you a clear picture of where carbon potential sits across your property and where focused management could build on the existing Strength Zones. sent_emails.subject: AgriProve - Farm Visit with Will Frecheville
sent_emails.body: Hi Mark, Thanks for giving Will the opportunity to come and discuss AgriProve as soil carbon developer. We hope you found the session informative while you are making your decisions on the direction you are heading with the potential of registering a project. I've attached your HORIZON: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=PHVIKD2MOV0 Snapshot, which shows the estimated opportunity based on our analysis of the property. You have 443 eligible hectares — 81.6% of the property — underpinned almost entirely by Dermosols, which provide moderate-to-high water holding capacity and productivity, creating conditions well-suited to carbon building. The analysis shows Strength Zones across the northern and north-eastern sections where modelled carbon levels currently sit above the property median, and Opportunity Zones through the central and western portions of the property where improved management practices could support meaningful gains. With 659mm of annual rainfall and 85% of the soil profile exceeding 60cm depth, there's real capacity for carbon storage in this landscape. We're projecting approximately 33,225 ACCUs over 25 years based on our rainfall band methodology — an estimated potential that supports 2 registered projects across the property. The eligible area shown is derived from automated satellite analysis and should be treated as a reference. Our geospatial team conducts a detailed property assessment as part of the next stage, combining expert interpretation with your on-ground knowledge. If you notice managed land that appears to have been excluded, our team will work together with you to review and, where appropriate, include it in your project area. Let me know when you'd like to jump on a call to talk it through. sent_emails.body: Hi Jon, Thanks for your time with Hobbs yesterday and your interest in exploring soil carbon for The Willows and your other prospective clients with your portfolio. I've attached your HORIZON Snapshot, which shows the estimated opportunity based on our analysis and amended the annual rainfall as rquested. You have 749 eligible hectares across the property, with Chromosol soils that create conditions suited to carbon building under improved management. The analysis shows Strength Zones scattered across the western paddocks, through the northern sections, and across the southern and eastern blocks where modeled carbon levels currently sit above the property median, and Opportunity Zones prominent across the northern paddocks and through central sections where targeted grazing management could support carbon gains. With 650mm of rainfall and soil depths reaching 2.1m across extensive areas, there's substantial capacity for carbon storage in the soil profile. The 82% eligibility rate is strong—satellite analysis excluded forests, infrastructure, and waterways, leaving 749 hectares of project-ready grazing land across your 911-hectare property. We're projecting approximately 56,175 ACCUs over 25 years based on our rainfall band methodology. At 749 eligible hectares, Growth Farms is well-positioned for two efficiently scaled projects (~400ha each). You're situated in a highly active region—approximately 40 neighboring properties across the Wagga Wagga-Tumut corridor are at various project stages, and credited projects within 50km are actively receiving credits, demonstrating these conditions support carbon building. sent_emails.subject: Your Key Commercial Terms - Important update from AgriProve
sent_emails.body: Hi Daniel, I hope the start of the has been treating you well. I'm reaching out because we've made some significant changes to AgriProve's Key Commercial Terms based on direct feedback from farmers like yourself. Your previous terms document has been paused while we bring everyone across to the new framework. The short version: we've listened to what producers have told us wasn't working, and we've fixed it. What's changed? • Your ACCUs, your account - We'll help you set up your own ANREU account. Once credits are generated, they sit with you, not us. You decide when and how to trade them. • Complete transparency on the 75/25 split - No more ambiguity. Your entitlement is explicitly calculated: total ACCUs × 75%, minus any owed for additional services. Simple maths, clear outcomes. • Exit pathway if numbers don't work - After baseline sampling (before year 5 reporting), we review results together. If the project doesn't stack up commercially, you can walk away with no further obligations. • Capped financial exposure - Clear 5-year limit on what you'd owe if ACCU generation doesn't cover baseline costs. No surprises down the track. • We're more accountable than ever before - If AgriProve doesn't deliver, you have defined pathways to replace us or exit entirely, with proper transition support. These changes are designed to remove that complexity. It would be valuable for a quick phone conversation to walk through what this means for your operation specifically so we can reissue your new Key Commercial Terms as soon as possible for your solicitor to have a look at. sent_emails.body: Hi Amanda and Pete, Thank you for working through the connectivity challenges the other week - we appreciate your patience and have reviewed the full recording to ensure we captured everything discussed (see attached) Key Outcomes from Our Discussion: 1. Financial Penalty Protection - Complete Peace of Mind Your land development activities (pine clearing and cropping conversion in the back paddock) will not result in any financial penalties. AgriProve accepts the risk of carbon stock fluctuations during these remediation activities. This is clearly documented in your land management strategy, and we're fully aligned with your approach. 2. Project Structure - Two Separate Projects You've confirmed preference for two projects, which offers the financial advantage of earlier ACCU generation: Grazing Project: Improved pasture establishment (digit + legume mix) Cropping Project: Fertilizer application This structure means whichever project shows carbon sequestration first will start generating ACCUs - potentially 1-2 years earlier than a combined project. 3. Eligible Activities Confirmed Improved pasture: Digit planted November, legume mix spread following March Fertilizer application: Tracked through existing agronomist records Grazing management remains available to add later if tracking becomes easier 4. Project Area Refinement We'll remove the narrow spurs and ridge line fingers from the project map to focus on areas you can practically manage with machinery. Small rock shelves encountered during development can be addressed through sampling adjustments - this won't impact the project. Within the main paddock areas, if you run equipment over land and encounter unexpected obstacles, we can either: Remove those specific areas during sampling Use grazing as the covering activity for irregular sections 5. Understanding Project Risks The only scenario requiring ACCU repayment would be if you chose to completely change land use (e.g., residential development) after ACCUs were issued. Your planned farming activities - including potential feedlot construction - can be accommodated by excluding specific areas from the project. There's no guarantee of carbon sequestration rates, but your multi-activity approach (pasture improvement + fertilizer) positions you well for success. 6. Activity Timeline - Flexible Approach You can develop improved pasture areas progressively over the 25-year project period. The requirement is simply that eligible activities cover the project area - this could be 50% improved pasture + 50% fertilizer application, for example. Once pasture is established, you maintain it rather than re-establishing annually. Lastly, are we able to get a quick picture of the areas that you want to exclude from the current project map? A quick screenshot with areas to cut out to speed up our operations process (rather than us assuming?) Thanks again and if you have any questions, please don't hesitate to let me know. sent_emails.body: Hi Tom and Rachel, Thank you both for taking the time to speak with me last while on the road to Sydney. I really appreciated the opportunity to learn more about your operations and discuss how AgriProve's: https://agriprove.io/ soil carbon program might align with your farm management practices. Based on our discussion, I wanted to confirm a few important aspects of how AgriProve's program works: What We Do (and Don't Do): We focus exclusively on soil carbon sequestration - no tree planting or land lock-up requirements You retain complete control over your farming decisions and land management We don't dictate agronomic practices or align with specific agronomists/products The program is farmer-led - you continue managing your properties as you see fit Your Properties: Your three properties totaling 4,000 hectares meet our criteria well. We typically work with properties above 300-400 hectares, and your average rainfall of 880mm is excellent for soil carbon projects (we've had success with rainfall as low as 340mm/year). Financial Structure: No upfront costs until baseline soil sampling We cover all ongoing costs: administration, registration, monitoring, mapping, and audits 75/25 split: You receive 75% of carbon credits (ACCUs), we receive 25% to cover all project costs We only get paid when you get paid - aligning our interests with yours. Project Flexibility: 25-year project term with a 5-year review point where you can assess progress and decide whether to continue If sequestration isn't occurring as expected, there's an exit pathway No penalties for carbon loss due to drought, fire, or other uncontrollable events - you simply resume earning credits from your highest watermark Multiple properties can be enrolled separately, so you receive credits as soon as the first property shows measurable increases Addressing Your Specific Concerns: Given Rachel's 38 years of agronomic experience and your long-term focus on rotational grazing and soil improvement, I understand your carbon levels may already be relatively high. This is where our Horizon: https://agriprove.io/in-the-news-old/mr-wsd-horizon-launch technology becomes valuable - it provides a desktop assessment of your specific soil carbon potential based on your property's characteristics, soil types, pH, and organic matter levels. Regarding your excellent work with lime application to address soil acidity (pH 4.3-4.4), this could potentially qualify as a materially different practice under the program if you're increasing application rates or expanding coverage areas. The key is that practices must be either: Brand new to the property, or Materially different from what you've done in the previous 7 years (e.g., increased application rates, different timing, expanded areas) Your rotational grazing practices over the past 50 years demonstrate strong land stewardship. Unlike previous consultants, we would never recommend fencing off your upland wetland or changing management approaches that are working well for you. Your use of livestock behavior as an indicator of paddock health is exactly the type of informed management that makes soil carbon projects successful. sent_emails.body: Hi Lee, I hope you had a great Christmas and New Years. I just wanted to let you know that we have completed the HORIZON analysis on Morocco.. At 12 projects of ~400ha each, the scale delivers operational efficiency advantages. Regional activity validates the approach. sent_emails.subject: RE: AgriProve  - Stoneybrook Carbon Project
sent_emails.body: Hi Amanda, I hope you're week is going well. Thank you for your detailed email and for taking the time over the Christmas break to think through the practicalities of the carbon project. Your questions aren't a problem at all - they're exactly what we need to work through together to get this right for your operation. I just wanted come back to you in relation to this email before we have a chat in due course, hopefully early next week? Let me address your concerns directly, starting with the most important one. Firstly, regarding your land development activities - Pine Clearing & Cropping Conversion I want to give you complete peace of mind on this: we have no concerns about your intended clearing and development activities in the back paddock area (the orange-shaded zone in your map). Given these activities will happen in the first reporting period before any ACCUs are issued, and because they're clearly documented as part of your land remediation strategy to ultimately sequester carbon, we consider ourselves fully informed and in agreement with your approach. There will be no financial penalty imposed on you at any stage. AgriProve will take on the risk of any fluctuation in carbon stocks while you conduct these essential remediation activities. This is your land, and these are the right management decisions to improve it long-term - we're here to support that, not constrain it. The photos you've provided show exactly what Claudia saw when she visited, and we understand the practical realities of working with pine regrowth and neglected country that needs proper development. Secondly, I just wanted to highlight the differences between registering one project vs two projects. I think this is where we need to be very transparent and get down in the weeds with things because the mathematics genuinely work in your favour with two projects. The Key Financial Advantage of Two Projects: Here's what really matters: the minute either project shows carbon sequestration, you start receiving ACCUs for that specific project - you don't have to wait for the whole property to average out. Your improved pasture areas (once established) may sequester carbon faster than cropping areas. With two projects, you could start earning ACCUs from the grazing project in year 2 or 3, even while the cropping areas are still being developed With one combined project, you'd have to wait until the average across everything hits the threshold - potentially delaying your first ACCU payments by 1-2 years It's like having two income streams instead of one - whichever performs first starts paying you. Why Two Projects Are Also Easier Than You Might Think: I know two projects sounds more complicated, but here's how it actually works in practice: Grazing Project - "Establishing or Rejuvenating Pasture" This captures exactly what you're planning: converting native pasture to improved pasture (digit + mixed species) Once you plant an area to improved pasture, that area is ticked off for the rest of the 25-year project You're not locked into legumes or specific species - you have complete freedom to plant whatever pasture mix works best Cropping Project - "Applying Nutrients to Address Material Deficiency" This covers your fertiliser program across cropping areas You're already tracking fertiliser applications through your agronomist and records. Straightforward annual reporting. The alternative - proving fertiliser is "materially different" from the previous 5 years across every paddock - is actually harder to demonstrate and maintain records for over 25 years. Sampling Costs: The soil sampling requirements are actually the same whether you have one project or two - it's based on total hectares and variability, not number of projects. So there's no additional cost here. sent_emails.body: Hi Elizabeth, I hope you are well. It was great to see that you have recently registered on the AgriProve’s FREE platform to assessment the potential of a soil carbon project. The platform provides farmers with a cutting-edge, science-based solution for managing their environmental impact and improving farm productivity. By seamlessly integrating soil carbon project assessments with emissions intensity evaluations, our platform empowers farmers to make informed decisions about land management. AgriProve: https://agriprove.io/, Australia’s leading soil carbon developer, focuses on a goal to streamline access to soil carbon projects for farmers and help farmers take the guesswork out of practice changes while generating additional income. AgriProve: https://agriprove.io/ has registered over 600+ projects with 75% share of all carbon projects in Australia and over 123,000+ ACCUs (carbon credits) issued over our journey with primary producers. We are also the first in Australia to deliver soil carbon credits to farmers in Australia. sent_emails.subject: Horizon Session and ANREU account
sent_emails.body: I hope you and the family had a great Christmas. I’m back on deck from the 12th of January but I wanted to make sure you had the video link of the Horizon session. See link provided.: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=bv_GcFnJGTg Also, as an FYI - we will be moving to a more regular position where all of our landholders and partners will be required to have their own ANREU account to hold their ACCUs (this is the same set up Adam Gunthorpe has for his ACCU's essentially) Setting up an ANREU account can be done via the CER's website; or we can do it on behalf of the landholder once your Key Commercial Terms have bene signed. https://cer.gov.au/online-systems/anreu-account-guidance: https://cer.gov.au/online-systems/anreu-account-guidance What this means, is we have a number of marking positives and offerings that can be put to the landholder. We can absolutely set up an ANREU account for you Landholder has full flexibility and autonomy of their ACCUs You can elect to sell either through AgriProve or on their own, or through another broker This avoids a brokerage fee or holding fee from AgriProve if they have their ACCUs transferred and broker through someone else. We will look for formalise a process for setting up these accounts, starting with our landholders who have already been issued credits, and then working through clients with a measured increase and then onto clients as a part of their onboarding/re-sampling. sent_emails.subject: Why Southern Queensland is Australia's carbon capital
sent_emails.body: Russell, It occurred to me I should better introduce AgriProve and what we actually do! We're Australia's leading soil carbon developer, providing regional farmers insights to increase productivity, enhance soil health, and generate a new revenue stream while doing it. engagements.subject: AgriProve Carbon Farming - Important links provided with next steps
engagements.body: Hi Leesa, Boyd and Michelle, Thanks again for our time last week, really appreciate the opportunity to discuss the potential of a soil carbon project with AgriProve. Below are a few of the links to that we discussed which will be useful to continue the conversation relating to the potential of a soil carbon project: Horizon (link provided, click here to view): https://agriprove.io/in-the-news-old/mr-wsd-horizon-launch As mentioned on our call, Horizon is a highly sophisticated, machine learning soil organic carbon model which is providing farmers unprecedented visibility into soil carbon, access to annual crediting cycles and unlocking a new era of data-driven farm profitability. Horizon webinar (link provided, click here to view): https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=bv_GcFnJGTg which was conducted late last year with over 180 registered attendees. This was great insight into what Horizon is and how it delivers monthly soil carbon insights and annual credit issuance to current and future registered projects. AgriProve Project Proposal: https://ap1.hubs.ly/y0xGt-0 which covers the questions that I can take you through as part of your tailored Land Management Strategy Call which are essentially the next steps in the process to ensure we are on the way to developing your Carbon Project Plan. This is the 45 minute call that I mentioned in our meeting last week. AgriProve Project Proposal - Farm Management.pdf: https://ap1.hubs.ly/y0xGw-0 which also formulates part of your tailored Carbon Project Plan. This document is to be filled in by Michelle and Boyd prior to confirming a time to go through the Land Management Strategy Call. AgriProve Case Studies (link provided, click here to view): https://agriprove.io/casestudies If there is anything else you need from me or Will, please don't hesitate to let either of us know and we'd be happy to support any questions moving forward. Lastly, I've provided a meeting link if you require a follow up at any stage between now and confirming a time to undertake the Land Management Strategy Call. 60 min, 30 min, and 15 min meeting: https://meetings-ap1.hubspot.com/ben2218 Regards, Ben Payne | Account Manager Phone: 1300 467 645: tel:{Phone} Mobile: 0403893668: tel:{Mobile} Email: ben@agriprove.io: mailto:{E-mail} Address: 1/601 Dean Street, Albury NSW 2640 www.agriprove.io: https://agriprove.io/ : https://www.linkedin.com/company/agriprove-pty-ltd/ : https://www.facebook.com/agriprove1/ : https://www.twitter.com/agriprove : https://www.youtube.com/channel/UCj6-LPG2-c5h5RUn5u8SuZw Here at AgriProve we care for your privacy. engagements.body: Hi Michelle, I hope you and Boyd are well and that the week has started well for you. I wanted to follow up on our land management strategy call from January 29th. We're making great progress with your project documentation, but I'm still waiting on a few key pieces of information before I can submit everything to our operations team. Outstanding Items: Project Name – We discussed this during our call, and you mentioned checking with Leesa about whether it should align with your grant funding. Have you had a chance to settle on a name? (Could be as simple as "Tansey Pastoral" or "Armstrong Creek", or something more creative!) Stocking Rate Details – You mentioned you have this information on hand but needed to pull it together. Specifically, I need: Current and historical stocking rates (DSE/LSU/AE per hectare) Duration of grazing periods Number of paddocks and their sizes/average size Rest and recovery periods Five-Year Farm Management History – This includes both the grazing history document and the horticultural management section (for your 19-hectare pecan orchard) Click here for the link to AgriProve Project Proposal - Farm Management.pdf: https://ap1.hubs.ly/y0zt0n0 Paddock Maps – These will help us with the mapping phase and understanding the boundaries for both your grazing and horticultural areas Land Title Confirmation – You were going to double-check which title the potential pivot irrigation would fall under (once confirmed) Once I receive these details, I'll finalize the land management strategy document and submit it to Will's operations team to develop your carbon project plan with the intent to register the project. Please don't hesitate to reach out if you have any questions or need clarification on any of these items. I'm here to help! On another note, our Head of Operations, Will Frecheville, is potentially available for a farm visit the week of February 23rd. This could be a great opportunity to walk through your property together, discuss your eligible activities in more detail, and answer any questions you might have. engagements.subject: Riverina soils might be worth more than you think
engagements.body: G'Day Jonathan, Ben from AgriProve here. I wanted to personally reach out, as a proud Albury-based business in the region, I thought you might be interested in what we're seeing happen right across the Riverina region. Soil types within the Riverina including Red-brown earths, Chromosols, Sodosols and transitional clay create a natural "carbon sink" where organic matter filters into clay aggregates and locks in for 20-50 years. Why This Matters for Carbon: The combination of your soil types, pH management and yearly rainfall combination generate a significant carbon opportunity If your farm is over 400 hectares and you want to chat further, feel free to call me on+61 483 921 562 , or do you have a time this week and would like to book in for a quick chat? engagements.body: Hi Jonathan, Thanks again. I'm running the HORIZON Snapshot analysis on your approx.. 900ha property now - should have the desktop results to you by Monday. Once you've had a chance to review the data, I wanted to flag an option: Hobbs Margaret is based in Albury for the next few months doing field research for AgriProve. He's a cattle producer/rancher from Texas who came to Australia because we're ahead of the US on soil carbon systems . He's currently ground-truthing our satellite model across properties in the Riverina. If the HORIZON results look promising and you want to dig deeper, Hobbs could come out and walk through the data with you on the ground. He'd verify the soil profile predictions against actual conditions and talk through what the projections mean for the planned to the specific operation. No pressure either way - I'll send the report first, then you can decide if the ground verification would be useful. No cost, no obligation. engagements.body: Hi Jon, Thanks for your time with Hobbs yesterday and your interest in exploring soil carbon for The Willows and your other prospective clients with your portfolio. I've attached your HORIZON Snapshot, which shows the estimated opportunity based on our analysis and amended the annual rainfall as rquested. You have 749 eligible hectares across the property, with Chromosol soils that create conditions suited to carbon building under improved management. The analysis shows Strength Zones scattered across the western paddocks, through the northern sections, and across the southern and eastern blocks where modeled carbon levels currently sit above the property median, and Opportunity Zones prominent across the northern paddocks and through central sections where targeted grazing management could support carbon gains. With 650mm of rainfall and soil depths reaching 2.1m across extensive areas, there's substantial capacity for carbon storage in the soil profile. The 82% eligibility rate is strong—satellite analysis excluded forests, infrastructure, and waterways, leaving 749 hectares of project-ready grazing land across your 911-hectare property. We're projecting approximately 56,175 ACCUs over 25 years based on our rainfall band methodology. At 749 eligible hectares, Growth Farms is well-positioned for two efficiently scaled projects (~400ha each). You're situated in a highly active region—approximately 40 neighboring properties across the Wagga Wagga-Tumut corridor are at various project stages, and credited projects within 50km are actively receiving credits, demonstrating these conditions support carbon building. Next steps will be focused on a tailored Land Management Strategy Call which is approx. 45 minutes to understand the properties history, current practices and how you would like to implement improved soil health practice with the intention of undertaking a soil carbon project with AgriProve. So we can arrange baseline soil sampling prior to Autumn, it would be great to lock in a time for the Land Management Strategy Call next week. Below is a link to schedule a time for this call. 60 min, 30 min, and 15 min meeting: https://meetings-ap1.hubspot.com/ben2218 If you have any questions, let me know and I'll touch base with you before the end of the week. engagements.subject: Re: Fwd: AgriProve - Farm Visit with Hobbs Margaret
engagements.body: Morning Jon, I hope you had a good weekend. We are now reading to issue you the Key Commercial Terms and Carbon Project Plan for Weatherall Carbon Project. Before I do so, I wanted to give you a heads up on a couple of things happening on our end before it lands with you. From 1 July, we're moving to a new mandatory baseline sampling configuration — 24 cores per Carbon Estimation Area, up from the current 12. This comes out of recent independent review work and improves project accuracy and reduces variance, so it's a sound change. But it does affect cost. At current per-core pricing, the difference looks like this: Current configuration (16 cores): ~$8,000 per CEA New configuration from 1 July (24 cores): ~$10,770 per CEA For anyone who has signed their Key Commercial Terms before 30 June, current pricing applies to their baselining. The original Weatherall HORIZON report quote was $12,608 which aligns with the standard 4x4 config for 2 projects. If we expand the number of cores to 6 per strata, the baseline cost becomes $17,664. The second thing worth flagging — if your property is in New South Wales, particularly the Riverina region, our sampling crew will be on the ground in May and June. If we can tie your baselining into that window, we can lock in a guaranteed date. After that, we genuinely can't say when we'll next be back in the region based on sampler availability and weather conditions — it could be 12 months away, which would push your first crediting cycle out accordingly. I'd rather you have the full picture now than find out later. Happy to run through what it means for your specific property if that's useful — just let me know a time that suits.
