engagements.body: Hi Brandon, Great to connect with you earlier today – and congrats again on the Holbrook property. Just wanted to follow up ahead of Hobbs' visit later in March. As I mentioned, Hobbs is across from Texas as part of a fellowship focused on learning from innovative producers here in Australia. To make the most of his time with you, it helps him to do a bit of homework on a the Holbrook beforehand – things like soil types, land capability, rainfall patterns and so on. That way the conversation on the day is a lot richer and more relevant to what you're actually working with on the ground. engagements.subject: NSW Farmer increases carry capacity AND generates ACCU's
engagements.body: Hi Kelly, Ben from AgriProve here. I wanted to personally reach out because, as a fellow NSW farmer, you might be interested in the story of John Lawson — a farmer in your region who has successfully generated soil carbon credits. Their story here: https://agriprove.io/killen-carbon-project. In under 2 years, using a combination of soil remediation practices and strategic land management they saw a massive 100% lift in carry capacity and earned 1,711 credits valued at over $61,000 at current ACCU price. That's over $630/ ha/ YEAR delivered straight to their bottom-line! engagements.subject: Riverina soils might be worth more than you think
engagements.body: G'Day Kelly, Ben from AgriProve here. I wanted to personally reach out, as a proud Albury-based business in the region, I thought you might be interested in what we're seeing happen right across the Riverina region. Soil types within the Riverina including Red-brown earths, Chromosols, Sodosols and transitional clay create a natural "carbon sink" where organic matter filters into clay aggregates and locks in for 20-50 years. engagements.subject: Kland Holdings — HORIZON Snapshot via Hobbs Margaret Farm Visit
engagements.body: Hi Kelly and Anthony, Thanks for your time last Friday with Hobbs. We appreciate you taking the time in your busy day to host him. We have now completed the HORIZON analysis across Kland Holdings and the numbers are worth paying attention to (see attached in this email or click here to view: https://www.canva.com/design/DAHED03d650/h3-25SBB9DyjS3AKuuXB_g/watch?utm_content=DAHED03d650&utm_campaign=designshare&utm_medium=link2&utm_source=uniquelinks&utlId=h153685c779) Here is what you are sitting on: Across 2,309 eligible hectares, Kland Holdings has an estimated 25-year ACCU potential of approximately 144,000 carbon credits. That is built on your existing grazing operation, on country you already manage, across 6 project areas of roughly 400 hectares each. The southern Riverina corridor is proven ground for AgriProve, with credited projects active in the surrounding region confirming this rainfall band and land type delivers real carbon outcomes. There is also something specific to your farming enterprise worth highlighting. Your HORIZON data shows consistent soil pH readings between 4.71 and 4.97 across the entire eligible area. That is a strongly acidic profile, and under the Emissions Reduction Fund soil carbon method, acid soil remediation through lime application is a recognized eligible activity. That means the pH story here is not a constraint. It is potentially an additional lever for carbon performance on top of grazing management. Why this works: AgriProve has registered soil carbon projects across southern NSW and the broader Riverina region. Active and credited projects in your corridor demonstrate that this climatic zone and soil type, managed well, generates measurable carbon gains and verified ACCUs. Your HORIZON Opportunity Zone coverage across the northern paddocks of both blocks tells us there is genuine room to move performance upward from the current baseline. What we handle: We take care of the complexity: sampling design, baseline field work (our team comes to you), laboratory analysis, ERF registration, ongoing reporting to the Clean Energy Regulator, subsequent sampling every 5 years, audit coordination, and ACCU issuance. Your role is providing property access and continuing the land management you are already doing. That is it. engagements.body: Hi Kelly and Anthony, Thanks for your time last Friday with Hobbs. We appreciate you taking the time in your busy day to host him. We have now completed the HORIZON analysis across Kland Holdings and the numbers are worth paying attention to (see attached in this email or click here to view: https://www.canva.com/design/DAHED03d650/h3-25SBB9DyjS3AKuuXB_g/watch?utm_content=DAHED03d650&utm_campaign=designshare&utm_medium=link2&utm_source=uniquelinks&utlId=h153685c779) Here is what you are sitting on: Across 2,309 eligible hectares, Kland Holdings has an estimated 25-year ACCU potential of approximately 144,000 carbon credits. That is built on your existing grazing operation, on country you already manage, across 6 project areas of roughly 400 hectares each. The southern Riverina corridor is proven ground for AgriProve, with credited projects active in the surrounding region confirming this rainfall band and land type delivers real carbon outcomes. There is also something specific to your farming enterprise worth highlighting. Your HORIZON data shows consistent soil pH readings between 4.71 and 4.97 across the entire eligible area. That is a strongly acidic profile, and under the Emissions Reduction Fund soil carbon method, acid soil remediation through lime application is a recognized eligible activity. That means the pH story here is not a constraint. It is potentially an additional lever for carbon performance on top of grazing management. Why this works: AgriProve has registered soil carbon projects across southern NSW and the broader Riverina region. Active and credited projects in your corridor demonstrate that this climatic zone and soil type, managed well, generates measurable carbon gains and verified ACCUs. Your HORIZON Opportunity Zone coverage across the northern paddocks of both blocks tells us there is genuine room to move performance upward from the current baseline. What we handle: We take care of the complexity: sampling design, baseline field work (our team comes to you), laboratory analysis, ERF registration, ongoing reporting to the Clean Energy Regulator, subsequent sampling every 5 years, audit coordination, and ACCU issuance. Your role is providing property access and continuing the land management you are already doing. That is it. The next step is a 45-minute call to confirm the project design and lock in your sampling slot. I have availability this Thursday or Friday afternoon. Does one of those work for you? engagements.subject: AgriProve soil carbon potential project  - Qualification Call
engagements.body: Hi Richard, Thanks again for the chat earlier today. If you had a chance to provide your lot and plan numbers and paddock maps prior to our catch up, that would be great. I wanted to ensure you have as much information and support from AgriProve as possible. AgriProve is Australia’s leading soil carbon developer with a focus on scalability and farmer-led solutions which simplifies the soil carbon journey, from implementation to earning ACCUs (carbon credits) AgriProve’s goal is to streamline access to soil carbon projects for farmers, and help farmers take the guesswork out of practice changes. Attached is a developer checklist is for your assistance as well. AgriProve has registered over 550+ projects with 75% share of all carbon projects in Australia and over 180,000 hectares under management. engagements.body: Hi Richard, Below are the restrictions on thinning and clearing in conjunction with a soil carbon project based on your questions around tree thinning within 5 years. Restricted/Prohibited Activities - Thinning and Clearing (2) Woody vegetation may be cleared only if: (a) any clearing is undertaken in accordance with any applicable regional natural resource management plan and Commonwealth, State, Territory or local government environmental and planning laws; and (b) at least one of the following apply: (i) the clearing is to manage woody horticulture crops, as part of standard business operations; (ii) the clearing is required to manage woody horticulture crop, following a disturbance; (iii) the clearing is to manage growth of a known weed species as defined in the CFI Regulations; (iv) the clearing is required to reduce the risk of fire; (v) the land was not forest cover in the 5 years prior to the lodgement of the section 22 application for the project or the section 29 application for the land. (3) Thinning of the land is only permitted if: (a) the thinning is to the extent necessary to comply with Commonwealth, State, Territory or local government environmental and planning laws; or (b) the thinning is of woody biomass to be used either: (i) as firewood for personal use and the carbon stock in the land after the thinning would not be more than 5% less than it would have been if the biomass was not thinned; or (ii) in accordance with traditional indigenous practices or native title rights; or (c) at least one of the following apply: (i) the thinning is to manage woody horticulture crop, as part of standard business operations; (ii) the thinning is required to manage woody horticulture crop, following a natural disturbance; (iii) the thinning is to manage growth of a known weed species as defined in the CFI Regulations; (iv) the thinning is required to reduce the risk of fire; Authorised Version F2021L01696 registered 02/12/2021 20 Carbon Credits (Carbon Farming Initiative—Estimation of Soil Organic Carbon Sequestration using Measurement and Models) Methodology Determination 2021 (v) the land was not forest cover in the 5 years prior to the lodgement of the section 22 application for the project or the section 29 application for the land. engagements.subject: Re: AgriProve - Nitrogen tool update
engagements.body: Hi Angus, I hope you have been keeping well. I understand your frustartion here and we are working as hard as we can to allow a commerically viable model for all partiers - landholder, developer and regulator alike. Currently no definative timeline as to when or what it will occur. The 400ha threshold isn't something AgriProve has set arbitrarily — it's driven by economics and the underlying methodology requirements rather than a hard regulatory rule. It's a legitimate question and I'd rather be straight with you than talk you into something that doesn't stack up. In low-rainfall country that number holds pretty firmly. High-rainfall country is a different story — the sequestration rates we see up there can shift the economics enough to make a smaller block work. I'd like to run a HORIZON Snapshot over your place before either of us calls it. It'll tell us your eligible area, what gets excluded, and whether it's actually worth pursuing. If it's not there, I'll tell you. All I need is your property name, land titles or lot and plan numbers — takes me a few days from there. engagements.subject: RE: New financial year, new soil carbon opportunity
engagements.body: Hi Daniel, I hope you are well. Just wanted to cover some of the final points with the Carbon Project Plan for Calca Block. My operation officer has just asked a few questions so we can get this issued to you: Please see below: Propose merging projects 1 and 2 on scrub country to allow for flexibility with paddock alterations and new fenceline positioning. This combined area can be registered as a single Carbon Estimation Area and subdivided into a number of strata so that we have adequate sampling density. This will simplify things in terms of record keeping and emissions accounting. See revised Project Area Confirmation map. Is fertiliser usage limited to the southern cropped areas only? Confirm whether any grazing areas have fertiliser applied. This eligible activity would then only apply to projects 2 & 3 (based on new config). Provide detail of cropping system management. If we can get Daniel to complete the table on page 11 of the attached Project Proposal doc. Provide detail on grazing practice over the cropped country? For how long on average and is it the whole mob? i.e. summer grazing of stubbles every year/second year, ~2,000 sheep for 3 months, dependent on available feed etc. For the information on grazing management in the playbook, does the 783 ha refer to the cropped areas of projects 2 and 3 to the south? Then 1,400 ha refer to the scrub pasture areas to the north? Have tillage passes in the baseline period been done strictly on the cropped areas? What is done on the scrub areas to the south in and around the cropped areas? Are sheep allowed to graze unrestricted on these areas when they are grazing stubbles? Based on satellite images and our knowledge of the region, presence of limestone/rock outcrops should be excluded from the project area. It would be good to gain further understanding of what the southern scrub areas are like in terms of rock/compaction and sampling ability and whether larger areas need to be excluded from the project. I can jump on a call and good through each question so we are well placed to finalise your Carbon Project Plan and Key Commercial Terms. engagements.subject: AgriProve - Introduction
engagements.body: Hi Tom, Thanks for the chat— I appreciated your time and the chance to talk through what soil carbon could mean for your operation. The short version: AgriProve exists to make soil carbon work for farmers — not the other way around. Our job is to take the complexity off your plate, maximize your credits, and make sure you're partnered with a developer you can trust for the long term. We've backed that up with results — 600+ registered projects, 75%+ market share of Australian soil carbon projects, and 123,000+ ACCUs issued to primary producers. We were the first to deliver soil carbon credits to Australian farmers and remain the fastest crediting developer in the market. What this means for your property: → A tailored project designed around your farming system → Annual crediting potential through our HORIZON: https://agriprove.io/in-the-news-old/mr-wsd-horizon-launch platform — no more waiting five years → Full transparency on your ACCU account and credit delivery → A dedicated specialist guiding you from eligibility through to income Key resources (click links provided below) → AgriProve Information Pack: https://ap1.hubs.ly/y0JcJN0 → Project Case Studies: https://agriprove.io/casestudies → Portfolio Map — see projects near you: https://maphub.net/danielwortmann/AgriProve-Portfolio-Australia → Eligible Practices & Building Carbon Guide: https://help.agriprove.io/what-is-a-soil-carbon-project → Create your free AgriProve platform account: https://app.agriprove.io/auth/signup As mentioned, we have a grazier in residence on the road with AgriProve at the moment that I'd love to arrange to come out your way for a short visit — an hour at most, entirely on your terms. engagements.subject: AgriProve - Farm Visit with Hobbs Margaret
engagements.body: Hi Jon, Thanks for your time with Hobbs yesterday and your interest in exploring soil carbon for The Willows and your other prospective clients with your portfolio. I've attached your HORIZON Snapshot, which shows the estimated opportunity based on our analysis and amended the annual rainfall as rquested. You have 749 eligible hectares across the property, with Chromosol soils that create conditions suited to carbon building under improved management. The analysis shows Strength Zones scattered across the western paddocks, through the northern sections, and across the southern and eastern blocks where modeled carbon levels currently sit above the property median, and Opportunity Zones prominent across the northern paddocks and through central sections where targeted grazing management could support carbon gains. With 650mm of rainfall and soil depths reaching 2.1m across extensive areas, there's substantial capacity for carbon storage in the soil profile. The 82% eligibility rate is strong—satellite analysis excluded forests, infrastructure, and waterways, leaving 749 hectares of project-ready grazing land across your 911-hectare property. We're projecting approximately 56,175 ACCUs over 25 years based on our rainfall band methodology. At 749 eligible hectares, Growth Farms is well-positioned for two efficiently scaled projects (~400ha each). You're situated in a highly active region—approximately 40 neighboring properties across the Wagga Wagga-Tumut corridor are at various project stages, and credited projects within 50km are actively receiving credits, demonstrating these conditions support carbon building. Next steps will be focused on a tailored Land Management Strategy Call which is approx. 45 minutes to understand the properties history, current practices and how you would like to implement improved soil health practice with the intention of undertaking a soil carbon project with AgriProve. So we can arrange baseline soil sampling prior to Autumn, it would be great to lock in a time for the Land Management Strategy Call next week. Below is a link to schedule a time for this call. 60 min, 30 min, and 15 min meeting: https://meetings-ap1.hubspot.com/ben2218 If you have any questions, let me know and I'll touch base with you before the end of the week. engagements.body: Morning Jon, I hope you had a good weekend. We are now reading to issue you the Key Commercial Terms and Carbon Project Plan for Weatherall Carbon Project. Before I do so, I wanted to give you a heads up on a couple of things happening on our end before it lands with you. From 1 July, we're moving to a new mandatory baseline sampling configuration — 24 cores per Carbon Estimation Area, up from the current 12. This comes out of recent independent review work and improves project accuracy and reduces variance, so it's a sound change. But it does affect cost. At current per-core pricing, the difference looks like this: Current configuration (16 cores): ~$8,000 per CEA New configuration from 1 July (24 cores): ~$10,770 per CEA For anyone who has signed their Key Commercial Terms before 30 June, current pricing applies to their baselining. The original Weatherall HORIZON report quote was $12,608 which aligns with the standard 4x4 config for 2 projects. If we expand the number of cores to 6 per strata, the baseline cost becomes $17,664. The second thing worth flagging — if your property is in New South Wales, particularly the Riverina region, our sampling crew will be on the ground in May and June. If we can tie your baselining into that window, we can lock in a guaranteed date. After that, we genuinely can't say when we'll next be back in the region based on sampler availability and weather conditions — it could be 12 months away, which would push your first crediting cycle out accordingly. I'd rather you have the full picture now than find out later. Happy to run through what it means for your specific property if that's useful — just let me know a time that suits. engagements.body: Hi Jon, Not a problem at all, great questions. See responses below: 1. What happens if carbon measurements decrease after ACCUs have been sold? This is about what the industry calls a "reversal" — where soil carbon levels drop below what was previously measured and credited. Under the ACCU Scheme, the Clean Energy Regulator can issue a relinquishment notice requiring ACCUs to be handed back if a reversal is detected. The key protection for landholders here is Clause 7.4 of the Master T&Cs, which states that AgriProve (as Project Proponent) is responsible for complying with any relinquishment notice except where the notice directly results from a breach of the agreement by the Landholder and/or Operator. In plain terms: If carbon levels drop due to normal variation, drought, or circumstances outside the landholder's control, AgriProve wears the relinquishment risk — not the landholder. This is one of the key commercial benefits of AgriProve acting as Project Proponent. If the drop is caused by the landholder breaching the agreement — for example, by undertaking Restricted Activities (Clause 2.4(3) and Attachment C) such as deep tillage or land clearing within the project area — liability can shift back to the landholder. The practical takeaway: as long as the landholder sticks to the Land Management Strategy and avoids Restricted Activities, the relinquishment risk sits with AgriProve. This is an important differentiator worth emphasising with clients. 2. Is the 25% AgriProve fee fixed, or can it move up or down? The short answer is: it can only move in the landholder's favour. The fee is set at 25% as established in the Key Commercial Terms. Under Clause 20.2 of the Master T&Cs, any amendments to the agreement cannot have a material adverse effect on the Landholder or Operator. An increase in AgriProve's fee from 25% would clearly constitute a material adverse effect, so it cannot be applied without written consent from all parties (Clause 20.4). The only automatic adjustment that can occur is downward. Under Clause 20.3, if AgriProve reduces its standard market offer below 25% (for example, to 20%), existing clients are automatically moved to the lower rate on a pro-rata basis from the next anniversary of the Start Date. So early adopters won't be locked into a higher fee if AgriProve's standard offering drops. In summary: the fee can go down if market conditions change, but it cannot go up without the landholder's written agreement. 3. Termination — what are the ramifications for ACCUs already sold? Termination mechanics are covered under Clause 13 of the Master T&Cs, and the implications differ depending on how and why the agreement is terminated. This only applies if the agreement is terminated and the project is revoked (deregistered) with the CER. There are mechanisms for a project to continue without AgriProve, where a project proponent is changed, or project activities are discontinued but the project continues on in an administrative capacity to eliminate the possibility of project deregistration. These are outlined below. If neither of these pathways are taken up, and a project agreement is terminated and the project is deregistered, then the following applies. The critical point is that ACCUs must have been issued to the project. The if a project is deregistered, then there is a regulatory requirement to relinquish ACCUs that have been issued to the project. Here's how it plays out under the main termination scenarios: No reasonable pathway (Clause 13.3): If both parties agree there's no viable path forward (i.e. that despite options presented in Clause 9 or Clause 14 the agreement/project must be terminated), the Operator must transfer back to AgriProve a number of ACCUs equivalent to all Project ACCUs issued to date (both the Operator's 75% and AgriProve's 25% share). engagements.body: Hi Ben, Thank you for the opportunity to assess the Bundaberg Sugar portfolio. I am pleased to share your HORIZON Snapshot, which covers the four eligible areas spanning the Burnett River corridor and coastal hinterland west and south of Bundaberg. See attached HORIZON Snapshot Report within this email and a click to view link provided here: https://www.canva.com/design/DAHEuM99fNU/6OcIF9EQ7iF8UsIp1mC0HA/watch?utm_content=DAHEuM99fNU&utm_campaign=designshare&utm_medium=link2&utm_source=uniquelinks&utlId=h02e1f5840b Here is what the analysis shows across your grazing country: Approximately 4,770 hectares of your portfolio is estimated as grazing-eligible for a soil carbon project under the Emissions Reduction Fund. Across that area, HORIZON has identified 12 potential projects with an estimated potential of around 596,250 ACCUs over a 25-year crediting period. That is a significant long-term asset layered directly over the grazing management you are already running. Your portfolio sits within the 1,001–1,100mm annual rainfall band, one of the strongest performance categories in the ERF framework, and your soils include Kandosol and Dermosol, which offer good water holding capacity and moderate to moderate-high carbon stability. The depth profile across the portfolio is particularly encouraging, with approximately 65% of your eligible area estimated at optimal depth of greater than one metre. Two confirmed AgriProve projects are operating within 20 kilometres of your eligible project area, which gives us confidence that this climate zone and management context supports measurable carbon outcomes. We take care of the complexity from here: sampling design, baseline field work (our team comes to you), laboratory analysis, ERF registration, ongoing reporting to the Clean Energy Regulator, subsequent sampling every five years, audit coordination, and ACCU issuance. Your role is providing property access and continuing the grazing management you are already doing. It is worth noting that the detailed boundary mapping between your grazing and sugar cane areas will be worked through by our operations team as part of the project design process, so the eligible area figures will be refined further at that stage. I would love to find a time to walk you through the snapshot and answer any questions. Would you be available for a call this week or next? Looking forward to partnering with you on this. engagements.subject: Re: KML of grazing areas
engagements.body: Hi Ben, Thank you for your patience while we worked through the detailed exclusion mapping for the Bundaberg Sugar portfolio. I am pleased to share your new HORIZON Snapshot, which now reflects the grazing-specific eligible areas across your four properties spanning the Burnett River corridor, coastal hinterland, and estuarine flats north and west of Bundaberg. Click to view link to the report also.: https://canva.link/uiu7nw2pywdh7gi Here is what the analysis shows: Your combined grazing-eligible area is 1,187.90 hectares across three estimated soil carbon projects, with an estimated potential of around 148,488 ACCUs over a 25-year crediting period. That is a meaningful long-term carbon asset built directly over the grazing management you are already running on this country. Your portfolio sits within the 1,001–1,100mm annual rainfall band, one of the strongest performance categories in the ERF framework. Soils across the portfolio are predominantly Sodosol, which responds well to gypsum application, one of the eligible management activities under the ERF soil carbon method. This gives your grazing country a clear and practical lever to build carbon performance over the project term. Approximately 60% of your eligible area is at optimal soil depth of greater than one metre, and pH across the portfolio ranges from 4.66 to 5.74, consistent with mildly to moderately acidic profiles that also open the door to lime application as an additional eligible activity. Two confirmed AgriProve projects are operating within 20 kilometres of the Bundaberg Sugar properties, which gives us confidence that this climate zone supports measurable carbon outcomes. On the economics, the baseline investment is straightforward at this scale: Option 1 involves a baseline sampling cost of $22,680 ex GST, with AgriProve's 25% success fee covering all ongoing project administration, sampling, auditing, and reporting across the project lifetime. Option 2 allows you to defer the full $22,680 baseline cost to be repaid from ACCUs generated within the first five years at $12.50 per ACCU, equivalent to 1,814 ACCUs. There is no upfront balance required under this option, with the 25% success fee applying as above. We take care of the complexity from here: sampling design, baseline field work (our team comes to you), laboratory analysis, ERF registration, ongoing reporting to the Clean Energy Regulator, subsequent sampling every five years, audit coordination, and ACCU issuance. Your role is providing property access and continuing the grazing management you are already doing. I would love to find a time to walk you through the snapshot and answer any questions. Would you be available for a call this week or next? We are also working quite closely with another sugar entity in Mackay that are looking are achieving very similar approaches that you are and I'll share a brief from them that might be the penny drop moment for our future interactions while we continue our discussions. Looking forward to your feedback and if you have any questions, let me know. engagements.subject: RE: KML of grazing areas
engagements.body: Hi Ben, You may have misinterpreted that one, but your concern is tottally understandable. Essentially, you can’t run a soil carbon project on a given area of land and convert that same land to environmental plantings for separate carbon credits. But you’re not locked out of environmental planting as a future avenue on different parts of their property, and the soil carbon project doesn't extinguish that optionality elsewhere on the farm. If there's any ambiguity about the eligibility of your specific land against the forest potential criteria, that's something I would flag with the project setup team to assess during the mapping and stratification process before registration. We would then get the soil carbon project mapped around the area you intended for environmental plantings and have the flexibility to move boundaries of the mapped project over the lifespan of the project. Hope this answers the question. Also, below is a brief that I have been working on with another sugarcane farm. I have applied XXXX for privacy of the client (I hope you don’t mind) that I’m also working on a project with. I thought this would be helpful for you to see. The Concept XXX farming system is built around a ~5-year cane rotation, with paddocks spending 12–18 months in fallow between cane crops. Rather than leaving fallow ground bare or under conventional management, XXXX returns those paddocks to multi-species pasture under high-density grazing, managed using E Shepherd (virtual fencing technology). The explicit goal of the pasture/fallow phase is to rebuild soil carbon before the paddock returns to cane production. Over a 25-year project period this would yield approximately 5 pasture rotations. His broader aims include: * Reducing reliance on synthetic inputs (fertiliser, chemicals) by rebuilding soil biology through the pasture phase * Incorporating robotics into the cane production phase for more precise input application * Using biodiversity monitoring robots to quantify ecosystem improvements alongside carbon * Proving the model on his own farm first, then rolling it out regionally with the data to back it up The expected carbon trajectory was discussed: carbon will increase during grazing/fallow phases and decline slightly during cropping phases, but the overall 25-year trajectory should be net positive — a "ladder" pattern where the incline outpaces the decline over time. ________________________________ Strategic Fit XXX has a strong interest in the platform play, data integration, and the suite of metrics AgriProve is building toward. This makes him not just a project opportunity but a potential proof-of-concept and regional advocate, given his connections across >5,000ha of regional cane. The opportunity is relatively small in isolation (XXXXha grazing component), but the bigger picture value lies in: * Proving the model works in a cane rotation system * Generating data that could underpin regional rollout * George's regional influence and connectivity as a pathway to scale ________________________________ Project Mechanics The registration and crediting structure needs careful sequencing given the rotation cycle: 1. Register the project while paddocks are still under cane — ideally just before the final harvest prior to entering fallow 2. Declare the project under cane so the declaration date is established 3. Baseline immediately upon entering fallow — so ACCU accumulation begins as soon as the carbon trajectory starts moving 4. Roll through each rotation — approximately every 5 years — repeating the process across the project life The key risk flagged by Will: don't baseline and then wait for fallow to begin, as you lose the benefit of capturing the full carbon increase from the start of the pasture phase. Timing the declaration right before the last cane harvest is the optimal approach. ________________________________ Next Steps A follow-up call has been scheduled for Friday April 10, The focus will be on: * Project mechanics…

engagements.subject: RE: KML of grazing areas
engagements.body: Thanks for clarifying that one. And yes, a decision we will have to make is weather to go down the road of soil carbon or do an environmental planting. The benefits for soil carbon farming is its low set up costs and comparable income to environmental plantings ACCU’s. The environmental planting benefits is that it keeps us open to the new biodiversity market opportunities for stacking. Interesting that you can have a flexible boundary built into soil carbon projects. Would that mean we could potentially establish soil carbon project and slowly reduce it over the years with tree planting? I get this could be counter intuitive as it takes time for carbon to build up in the soil. That is interesting with the cane farming. As I have been looking into stacked markets, would that allow this cane farmer to potentially stack reef credits on top of soil carbon credits under a reduced nitrogen application? Our current practice is to plant a soybean cover crop during fallow periods. Our fallow period does not last that long usually though. So if we were to pursue something similar we would have a land management practice change. Another recommendation I will be presenting to management is to pursue reduced nitrogen application for reef credits under a green collar project for our sugar cane land. This has a lot of potential for us as we have a lot of cane land sitting on major waterways that drain onto the southern great barrier reef. Could soil carbon stack on top of this under the sugar cane soil carbon idea? I guess it’s the same idea as above but just with the emphasis on generating reef credits with a side bonus of soil credits rather than the other way around. engagements.body: Hi Dean, Good question, and one that comes up fairly regularly given the political landscape around carbon markets. Our Agreement covers this - "question posed to the Key Commercial Terms Project: What happens if there is a change of Government and how is the agreement impacted?: Short answer: A change of government doesn't automatically affect existing agreements. The ACCU scheme (ERF/Carbon Credit scheme) was started in 2011 - and has been through multiple government changes - so it is likely that it will remain, it may change form; but unlikely to be scrapped entirely. Historical context worth knowing The ACCU Scheme has survived multiple changes of government, including the Abbott Government's repeal of the carbon price in 2014 — the ERF/ACCU Scheme itself was actually introduced by that same government as a replacement. There is now broad bipartisan support for the scheme's continued operation, which reduces this risk considerably compared to a decade ago. What the agreement says The Master Terms and Conditions (attached) addresses this scenario directly in clause 13.6, which deals with changes to Relevant Law: If there is a change of Relevant Law that has the effect that the Carbon Projects will no longer be eligible to receive ACCUs or carbon credits under another comparable program, then either party may terminate the Agreement once any existing sale, transfer or payment obligations have been fulfilled. "Relevant Laws" is defined broadly in the definitions section to cover all laws relevant to the Carbon Projects, including the CFI Act, ANREU Act, and requirements of any regulatory authority. engagements.subject: Your HORIZON Snapshot – Jonsson Farms -  Ravenshoe
engagements.body: Hi Dean, Thanks again for the chat today. I've put together your HORIZON Snapshot, which maps out the soil carbon potential across your 116 eligible hectares at Evelyn Central, Ravenshoe QLD. A few things stand out from the analysis that are worth highlighting. Your soils are exceptional. The entire eligible area is mapped as Ferrosol, a soil classification that rates high across water holding capacity, productivity, and carbon stability. Combined with 1,500mm of annual rainfall and soil depths running from 1.00 to 1.44 metres across the whole property, the Ravenshoe parcel has the kind of profile that performs well over a long crediting period. At a pasture rate of 6.0 ACCUs per hectare per year, the 25-year potential for this parcel sits at approximately 17,415 ACCUs as part of your broader Jonsson Farms project portfolio. That is a meaningful contribution from 116 hectares. On the economics, the baseline sampling cost for one project across 116 hectares comes to $7,984 (ex GST), with the option to defer that cost entirely and repay via 639 ACCUs generated in the first five years. engagements.body: Hi Dean, Great speaking with you today — it's exciting to see [Property Name] moving toward project registration. There are three things that will help us hit the ground running: Paddock maps for each property — digital files are ideal, but hand-drawn maps showing clear boundary lines work just as well. These let us accurately configure your project areas before the call. Five-year farm management history: https://ap1.hubs.ly/y0Hr-W0 — this is one of the most important pieces of the puzzle. To accurately model your soil carbon baseline and project what your land can sequester, we need a clear picture of how your properties have been managed over the past five years. Think stocking rates, pasture management, any significant land use changes — the more detail the better. Don't worry if it's not perfectly documented; we'll work through it together on the call. The AgriProve Project Proposal (Farm Management): https://ap1.hubs.ly/y0HrZ-0 — I've attached this document and linked it below. It's the foundation of our conversation, so the more detail you can fill in beforehand, the more productive our session will be. If you run into any questions while working through it, just send them through. Our Land Management Strategy Call runs around 45 minutes. We'll work through the project proposal together, assess your properties, and map out a clear path to registration. engagements.subject: Your HORIZON Snapshot — Hunter Valley Wagyu Weemala
engagements.body: Hi James, I hope you're well. I'm pleased to share your HORIZON Snapshot for your first property, Weemala. I've attached the full Snapshot for your review and provided a click to the link HORIZON Snapshot here: https://canva.link/jtril8tgd6g74j6. The analysis has identified 58.77 hectares as eligible for a soil carbon project, representing 78.9% of the property. At 1,328 mm of annual rainfall, Weemala sits in our highest ACCU rate band, giving the property an estimated potential of around 8,816 ACCUs over a standard 25-year crediting period. The HORIZON map reveals a strong base of carbon performance across the western and central-western paddocks, with meaningful Opportunity Zones through the eastern and southern areas where targeted grazing management could lift performance further. There is also a notable soil health story at Weemala. The pH data shows strongly acidic conditions across the full eligible area (4.53 to 4.76), and lime application and acid soil remediation are both eligible activities under the ERF. This opens a practical conversation about layering soil health improvement alongside the carbon project, with the costs of those activities potentially supported through the program. As mentioned in our previous conversations, at 58.77 eligible hectares, Weemala sits below the standalone project registration threshold under the ERF. On its own, the property isn't quite large enough to register as an independent project. The good news is that this is a straightforward pathway to resolve, and one we work through with landholders regularly. Combined eligible area across your other properties brings the project to the required scale, and Weemala's high-rainfall, high-rate contribution becomes a meaningful part of a larger, commercially viable whole. Mountain Creek, NSW 2644 DP 191083,Lot 4;6 DP 224023 Tarcoola, 1545 Mountain Creek Rd., MOuntain Creek, NSW 2644. Lot 2 DP 224024 Please list all landowners full names, emails, phone numbers Notes: Name(s) William Cottrell Email: will.cottrell1967@gmail.com Phone: 0407360463 Please provide a brief history of your farm The property, known as Tarcoola, is situated on approximately 534.1 hectares located on Mountain Creek. The Cottrell family has owned and managed the property across multiple generations, with William Thomas Gregory Cottrell assuming management of the property at the age of 27 following the passing of his father. The property was historically managed as a sheep enterprise, before transitioning into a partnership operation running Shorthorn cattle. Approximately ten to twelve years ago, the enterprise shifted from a Shorthorn breeding operation into a cattle trading system. Concurrent with the move to cattle trading, cropping was introduced to the property for the purpose of producing feed for the fattening of trading cattle, rather than for commercial grain production. Please provide a brief description of your background, any relevant accreditations, skills and experience and any ongoing training that assist in managing the land: [Please include any current agronomic advice] William Cottrell has been involved in farming from approximately ten to twelve years of age, having grown up on the property. Upon leaving school, William undertook a farm management and wool classing course. His knowledge and expertise is predominantly self-taught, built through decades of practical experience managing livestock, including sheep and cattle, and broadacre cropping systems. William is a member of the local Landcare organisation, which provides a regular channel for information on land management and conservation practices. William has extensive practical experience in livestock husbandry and stock handling across his entire farming career. Please provide a summary of your soil carbon project philosophy and goals: William's approach to the carbon project will focus on creating optimal conditions for soil carbon sequestration and productive grazing, both of which will promote each other in a positive feedback loop. This involves a commitment to specific eligible activities which are detailed in Section 4. The goal will be to improve soil structure, water retention, soil health, and biological activity, which both builds carbon levels and increases primary productivity. By engaging in a long-term soil carbon project, William will be able to continually monitor and receive feedback on land management practices, providing insights that would otherwise not be possible. Do you use any farm management software or digital tools? Or do you have any plans to implement any additional solutions to assist with record keeping? What do you currently use for monitoring and record keeping? The operation utilises Xero for accounting purposes. engagements.body: Hi Ben Thanks for your call yesterday, apologies I was sleeping off night shift and probably sounded as such! We have got back home now after a fairly ordinary month of being away. With a death in the family comes change- change which we certainly were not foreseeing anywhere on our radar any time soon. Now that Mum is gone, Dad is unsure of his future on their property alone as he also ages. The next 12months will give us all a bit of time to process and think about what the future might look like and potentially put plans in place- but one highly likely scenario that is being talked about is the sale of both our property and my father’s to consolidate into one property somewhere likely in QLD where we can continue our business ventures but also look after Dad living on the same property as he ages and maintains involvement in agriculture for as long as he is physically able to. Therefore, I think it would be unwise for us to move ahead any further with signing up to a soil carbon project at this stage when our property may be going on the market before ticking the boxes for the eligible activities being done. I know we have put a lot of work into the back and forth of trying to understand the carbon concepts and especially get the mapping side correct; and I am not saying it is off the table forever as it is something we are very much interested in proceeding with; however given the change in direction of our family I think we should just pause now and let some time go by until decisions are made. engagements.subject: Re: AgriProve Soil Carbon Project - Introduction
engagements.body: Hi Dan, Thank you for the opportunity to run the HORIZON analysis across your additional Home Block at Mount Tom. I've attached your HORIZON Snapshot (click to link provided also: https://www.canva.com/design/DAHDmHbkPQM/gMKzVnM4uZDs8TLtPfjNIg/watch?utm_content=DAHDmHbkPQM&utm_campaign=designshare&utm_medium=link2&utm_source=uniquelinks&utlId=h1f6ce7bb8f), and wanted to walk you through what it shows and what it means for your property. What the analysis found: HORIZON has identified 142.94 hectares of eligible land across your 305.49 ha property, sitting within the Miriam Vale coastal hinterland at 1,050mm annual rainfall. At that rainfall level, your land falls into our highest ACCU rate tier, with an estimated potential of 5.0 credits per hectare per year. Over a 25-year crediting period, that points to an estimated 17,868 ACCUs gross from this block. The zone map shows a mixed picture across your eligible area, with Strength Zones concentrated along the western fringe and southern boundary, and Opportunity Zones broadly spread through the central and eastern sections. That spread tells us there is meaningful room to lift carbon performance across the property through adjusted grazing management, and your strongest country provides a solid foundation to build from. A candid note on scale: I want to be straightforward with you. At 142.94 eligible hectares, this block sits below the usual standalone threshold we typically require to register a project under the ERF soil carbon method. That is not a reflection of your land's carbon potential, which is genuine, but rather a practical constraint of project economics and regulatory design. The good news is that, with the additional land under separate title or management, those areas could be assessed and combined with this block to reach a viable project scale. In the meantime, your HORIZON Snapshot gives you something genuinely useful regardless of the project pathway. The zone maps, soil depth data, and carbon distribution analysis are a practical tool for understanding where your land is performing and where targeted management could make a difference. I would love to have a conversation about what the options look like for your situation. Would you have time for a quick call in the next week? Happy to work around what suits you. engagements.subject: Your HORIZON Snapshot — Lilymere Agriculture
engagements.body: Hi Erin, Thank you for your interest in AgriProve's soil carbon project. I'm pleased to share your HORIZON Snapshot for Lilymere Agriculture click here to view link: https://canva.link/fm2bfew0a918cnt, which gives you a detailed picture of your property's soil carbon profile and the opportunity it holds. Our HORIZON model has mapped 67.70 hectares of eligible area across your Glen William property, representing 56.8% of your land. The analysis shows a strong soil depth profile across the eligible area, ranging from 0.63 to 2.10 metres with no shallow or constrained country, which is a positive indicator for carbon sequestration potential. At 850mm annual rainfall, your property sits in AgriProve's 4.0 ACCU per hectare per year estimation band. Over a standard 25-year crediting period, your eligible area could support the generation of approximately 6,770 ACCUs. Your Kurosol soils carry moderate water holding capacity and carbon stability, and the depth and rainfall combination provides a genuine foundation to build from. One thing worth discussing when we connect is your soil pH. The HORIZON data shows your eligible area is running at pH 4.47–4.64 across the board, which sits in the strongly acidic range. Lime application to remediate acid soils is an ERF-eligible project activity, so there's a practical conversation to be had about how a carbon project can complement soil health improvements you may already be considering. AgriProve has active and credited projects operating across the Hunter Valley corridor, including a credited project approximately 8–10km to the northwest. This region has a demonstrated track record for measuring and generating verified soil carbon credits, and Lilymere Agriculture is well-positioned within that context. The attached HORIZON Snapshot outlines everything relevant to a potential soil carbon project. Beyond the baseline, AgriProve handles everything: sampling design, field work (our team comes to you), laboratory analysis, ERF registration, Clean Energy Regulator reporting, subsequent sampling every five years, audit coordination, and ACCU issuance. Your role is providing property access and continuing the land management you're already doing. I look forward to seeing you this Friday to go through the Snapshot and answer any questions you have. engagements.subject: Restrictions realting to irrigation for your carbon projects:
engagements.body: Hi Jason, Thanks again for today. A summary of the issues relating to irrigation for your carbon projects: Irrigation is a restricted activity under s.12(8) of the Methodology After completion of the baseline sampling round, irrigation may be applied to CEAs (Carbon Estimation Areas) within a project area only if both of the following apply: disregarding new irrigation, the annual level of irrigation for the project area is not more than 20% greater than the highest annual level of irrigation in the baseline period; disregarding new irrigation, the 5-yearly total level of irrigation for the project area is not more than 20% greater than the total level of irrigation in the baseline period. For example, if there was 10ML of irrigation applied in 2020, 5ML of irrigation in 2021 and none during the other baseline years, the project/CEA is restricted to: Using no more than 12ML of irrigation in any 1 year, and Using no more than 18ML in a 5-year period. 'New irrigation' is defined as “new or additional irrigation applied to land in a project area using water obtained through irrigation efficiency savings made after the date on which the section 27 declaration of the project was made” and is a result of improving the efficiency of irrigated water through one or both of the following: (i) on-farm irrigation infrastructure located within the project area; (ii) management practices within the project area This means that ‘new irrigation’ is essentially a redistribution of irrigation derived from efficiency savings, not simply applying more water. There is no restriction on how the water is redistributed, for example to other parts of the CEA under new irrigation infrastructure, so long as the water is derived from those efficiency savings. Hope that adresses your question and let me know if you have any others. engagements.subject: RE: HORZION Introduction from AgriProve
engagements.body: Hi Paul, It was great reconnecting with you and sorry it's taken a few weeks to come back to you. I've put together your new HORIZON Snapshot for Paul Webster Pastoral, which I've attached to this email.Also a clickable link provided here: https://www.canva.com/design/DAHE6CcLLbM/GCwGoCchg3wNE2uh9dg7JQ/watch?utm_content=DAHE6CcLLbM&utm_campaign=designshare&utm_medium=link2&utm_source=uniquelinks&utlId=h2120de5500. The analysis covers both properties and identifies approximately 360 hectares of eligible area across the properties, representing 63% of your total land. HORIZON has mapped how carbon is currently distributed across your landscape, giving us a clear picture of where your stronger country sits and where the most significant opportunity lies. A few things worth highlighting from the analysis: Your southern property shows genuine Strength Zone presence through its central and eastern sections, indicating carbon levels above your property median. This is encouraging. The northern property is dominated by Opportunity Zones, which reflects where targeted grazing management has the most capacity to lift carbon performance over time. Your soils are Dermosol and Sodosol across the eligible area, with a rainfall average of 725mm. At an estimated rate of 3.5 ACCUs per hectare per year, the property has a projected potential of approximately 31,479 ACCUs over a 25-year crediting period. Baseline sampling is estimated at $7,984 ex GST, with the option to defer that cost entirely against future ACCUs if preferred. The steep country soon prompted the Burnhams to question their management style and encouraged them towards regenerative grazing. The resulting increase in groundcover from an initially cautious beginning has solidified into a deep belief in regenerative grazing methods. Stonehaven and Glenroy have been certified USDA NOP organic, Biodynamic since 2015 and Grassfed certified through Teys program at its inception. The properties are also becoming Regenerative Certified from 2025. The Burnhams currently have a vegetation project underway (avoided clearing) with Green Collar in the last 5 years of 200 hectares. Emma-Jane has been a teacher for her working life and also comes from a beef production family. engagements.body: Hi Dan, I hope you're well. As an FYI - we will be likely moving to a more regular position where all of our landholders and partners will be required to have their own ANREU account to hold their ACCUs (this is the same set up Adam Gunthorpe has for his ACCU's essentially) Setting up an ANREU account can be done via the CER's website; or we can do it on behalf of the landholder once your Key Commercial Terms have bene signed. https://cer.gov.au/online-systems/anreu-account-guidance: https://cer.gov.au/online-systems/anreu-account-guidance What this means, is we have a number of marking positives and offerings that can be put to the landholder. We can absolutely set up an ANREU account for you Landholder has full flexibility and autonomy of their ACCUs You can elect to sell either through AgriProve or on their own, or through another broker This avoids a brokerage fee or holding fee from AgriProve if they have their ACCUs transferred and broker through someone else. We will look for formalise a process for setting up these accounts, starting with our landholders who have already been issued credits, and then working through clients with a measured increase and then onto clients as a part of their onboarding/re-sampling. engagements.subject: RE: Feedback from solicitors
engagements.body: Hi Dan and Emma-Jane, Thank-you again for taking the time to meet with me on Tuesday. I greatly appreciated the visit and the opportunity to discuss in further detail the Stonehaven Soil Carbon Project. Following up on our conversations and the actions that I have committed to you from that meeting, please see below: Action Item: Clarifications to clauses 13.3 and 14.3 to align with the explanations in the letter. This is a two part approach, firstly, we are happy to include these explanations as an appendix to the Key Commercial Terms, that we can sign-off and agree on. Clarification of Project Termination (once again, happy to include this into the appendix, so that it is agreed and signed). 13. Default and Termination 13.1 Where there is an Event of Default which is not remedied within 30 Business Days the non-defaulting party may choose to terminate this Agreement by giving written notice to the defaulting party. Event of Default means: (1) a material breach of this Agreement; (2) any failure to pay any amount or transfer any ACCUs in accordance with the Agreement; or (3) an Insolvency Event. 13.3 states: “Operator may terminate this Agreement if the parties, acting in good faith, agree there is no reasonable pathway to keep the Carbon Projects operational. In such circumstances, the Operator must: …” Under the Default and Termination clause, and assuming the agreement has not been terminated in line with Clause 2.3 (i.e. the project in unviable prior to the first reporting and issuance of ACCUs), AgriProve does not have rights to terminate the agreement. Clause 13.3 requires that both parties agree to terminate the project while acting in good faith. If AgriProve were to instigate and insist on a project termination due to our assessment that it was unviable for AgriProve to continue, you as a landholder/operator have the rights within this agreement to deny that termination of the project. If AgriProve were to continue down this path without your consent, then it would be likely be determined that we would be in breach of our good faith obligations, and that would constitute a material breach of the agreement. We would then be required to pay all costs associated and outlined as per 13.2. If the project was revoked, it would be our responsibility to return all ACCUs to the project, as we would have materially breached the agreement. This is of course, under the assumption that you as a landholder have: * Complied with all obligations under the LMS and Methodology * Reasonably believe the project remains viable for your business * Declines to agree that the termination is necessary. The second part, are the following drafted clauses: Amendment to 13.3(2) - (2) pay all outstanding fees and costs owed to AgriProve including the equivalent dollar value of any Additional Product and Services Fee ACCUs previously agreed. For the avoidance of doubt, where no Project ACCUs have been issued to the Carbon Projects as at the date of termination under this clause 13.3, and any baseline soil sampling costs have been met by the Operator in accordance with clause 8.2, no further fees or costs shall be payable by the Operator or Landholder to AgriProve; Lastly, and as discussed, it is not in our interest to revoke projects, this is out of line with our business strategy. If there was no pathway for our relationship to continue, and operate the project, then it would be transferring the project proponent and removal of AgriProve from project operation as per Clause 9. Please let me know any feedback following the above, and we can progress. I think (outside of the previously updated clauses (Biosecurity)) and the amendment to 13.3(2), the simplest option rather than re-drafting clauses, is to add the explanations and statements made in these emails as an appendix, and if approved, we can incorporate as an appendix to the KCT; so it is clear and agreed. engagements.subject: Following up on our conversation yesterday
engagements.body: HI Brian, Thanks for your time on the phone yesterday, I want to ensure that I can provide the clarity and transparency you raised in our call. The use of "may" in the agreement is there to provide flexibility to adapt internal process or actions as the project develops in practice, rather than committing to a process that may not suit the conditions on the ground. It is not there to show a lack of commitment or be uncertain for what we deliver. It also reflects something that is true of soil carbon broadly: we cannot provide guarantee on what any project will return, and we won't claim that we can. What the agreement does commit to unconditionally are the services we deliver: All soil sampling after baseline (you only pay for the initial baseline sampling) Project design and onboarding Soil results analysis and presentation, including all Method calculations Registration, monitoring, reporting and audit management ACCU issuance and distribution to you If there are specific clauses that still read as uncommitted, please flag them and we'll walk through each one directly. This is a shared model. Your risk is the upfront cost of baseline sampling, and the commitment to make improvements to your farming operation for soil carbon purposes — with no guarantee those activities will produce ACCUs that offset that cost. From that point, the risk sits with AgriProve. We operate on a success fee — if no credits are generated, we don't get paid. All costs, both time and financial, for reporting, sampling coordination, project design, monitoring and measurement across the first five-year period are borne by us. We also manage the relationship with the Clean Energy Regulator, including the responsibility to relinquish credits if requested. The only circumstance in which that obligation can be passed back to you is if you have materially breached the agreement. This carries through for the life of the project, whereby we will commit to completing the work and if there are no ACCUs we do not get paid. The 25-year term is a requirement of the ACCU scheme — it applies to every registered project, not just AgriProve's. There are genuine exit points along the way. Prior to ACCUs being awarded to your project, you can elect to discontinue at any time and for any reason. If you exit within that five-year window, the only cost is that the baseline sampling cannot be recovered through the scheme. There is no further obligation to AgriProve or the Clean Energy Regulator. We provide annual reports and assessments leading into the five-year review so there are no surprises — you'll have a clear picture of whether your project is tracking well before that decision point arrives. There are additional options once ACCUs have been issued, that we can walk through should this be of concern. Lastly, Government concerns. This is a fair and legitimate concern. The straightforward answer is that no one can guarantee what any government does over a 25-year period. What we can tell you is that a registered soil carbon project sits inside a legal framework that creates real barriers to retrospective change. Your project, once registered, is a legally binding contract with the Clean Energy Regulator and Australian Government. Any material change to the scheme would carry significant legal and financial implications for the government, which is why historically, changes to the ACCU scheme have applied to projects registered going forward, not to projects already registered. Our agreement also contains force majeure provisions that apply in the event of a material change to the relevant law, meaning if the scheme were changed in a way that fundamentally affected your project, there are provisions to exit the project. Beyond the legal framework, the ACCU scheme now has substantial institutional and corporate investment behind it. Demand for Australian carbon offsets from corporates meeting their own net zero commitments exists independently of government policy and is…

engagements.body: Hi Richard, Below are the restrictions on thinning and clearing in conjunction with a soil carbon project based on your questions around tree thinning within 5 years. Restricted/Prohibited Activities - Thinning and Clearing (2) Woody vegetation may be cleared only if: (a) any clearing is undertaken in accordance with any applicable regional natural resource management plan and Commonwealth, State, Territory or local government environmental and planning laws; and (b) at least one of the following apply: (i) the clearing is to manage woody horticulture crops, as part of standard business operations; (ii) the clearing is required to manage woody horticulture crop, following a disturbance; (iii) the clearing is to manage growth of a known weed species as defined in the CFI Regulations; (iv) the clearing is required to reduce the risk of fire; (v) the land was not forest cover in the 5 years prior to the lodgement of the section 22 application for the project or the section 29 application for the land. (3) Thinning of the land is only permitted if: (a) the thinning is to the extent necessary to comply with Commonwealth, State, Territory or local government environmental and planning laws; or (b) the thinning is of woody biomass to be used either: (i) as firewood for personal use and the carbon stock in the land after the thinning would not be more than 5% less than it would have been if the biomass was not thinned; or (ii) in accordance with traditional indigenous practices or native title rights; or (c) at least one of the following apply: (i) the thinning is to manage woody horticulture crop, as part of standard business operations; (ii) the thinning is required to manage woody horticulture crop, following a natural disturbance; (iii) the thinning is to manage growth of a known weed species as defined in the CFI Regulations; (iv) the thinning is required to reduce the risk of fire; Authorised Version F2021L01696 registered 02/12/2021 20 Carbon Credits (Carbon Farming Initiative—Estimation of Soil Organic Carbon Sequestration using Measurement and Models) Methodology Determination 2021 (v) the land was not forest cover in the 5 years prior to the lodgement of the section 22 application for the project or the section 29 application for the land. AgriProve Project Proposal Playbook Please list all operators full names, emails, phone numbers Notes: Name: Richard Cox Phone: 0409721830 Email: richard@cracowstation.com Name: Sarah Kate Cox Phone: 0418 152 859 Email: sarah@cracowstation.com Land Titles: 11/DW215 23/DW516 Please list all landowners full names, emails, phone numbers Notes: Name: Richard Cox Phone: 0409721830 Email: richard@cracowstation.com Please provide a brief history of your farm Krakow Station has been in Sarah’s family for approximately a century (“in my wife’s family … for 123 years”). Richard and Sarah assumed ownership and day-to-day management roughly twenty-two years ago (around 2004). The enterprise has always been grazing. Historically the station functioned as a 600 head breeder block, with cattle transferred to other properties. Over the past two decades the managers have focused on rebuilding the herd, improving water security and paddock layout, and progressively investing in infrastructure to support planned grazing. A smaller block that was resumed for mining in the 1960s was bought back by the family ~15 years ago and is now managed with the rest of the holding .Cracow Station has been in the family for 122 years. Always been grazing operation. Richard and Sarah have also implemented an 8 year Cap X program. Please provide a brief description of your background, any relevant accreditations, skills and experience and any ongoing training that assist in managing the land: [Please include any current agronomic advice] Richard was born on a cattle station in West Africa. Richard’s background is in pastoral operations. He completed station training and worked across northern Australia, including stock and management roles (e.g. Stanbroke) and a period in the United States with a diversified ranch family, gaining exposure to multiple on-farm enterprises. He is active in producer networks and research/producer representation (e.g., “producer rep on the managing … committee” noted), and is engaged with grazing education such as RCS/Andrews-style rehydration (natural sequence) concepts. Richard emphasizes stockmanship and dog handling, noting animal calmness and weight gain as key levers. Also completed the Stuart Andrews course. The business runs to a written, staged, eight-year capital works plan to spread risk across seasons while incrementally improving pastures, fencing, water and grazing control. No specific agronomist of record was named in the call; fertilizer and lime are not currently applied in the project area. Please provide a summary of your soil carbon project philosophy and goals: Richard's soil carbon project philosophy and goals treats soil carbon as a long-term measurement and feedback tool aligned with production. The philosophy is to improve soil structure, water distribution and retention, biological function and groundcover through planned grazing, legume establishment and landscape rehydration. Monitoring over time is intended to validate that capital investments and management changes are improving both productivity and soil condition. Do you use any farm management software or digital tools? Or do you have any plans to implement any additional solutions to assist with record keeping? What do you currently use for monitoring and record keeping? At the moment, Phoenix is used for mapping and accounting. Stock numbers and drafting/weighing are handled with Gallagher hardware plus spreadsheets. The business continuously evaluates software options but has not yet found a perfect fit; upgrades are being considered as grazing control increases. Do you use any predictive modelling to assist in management decisions? Yes—Richard KLR Marketing tools (referred to as “KLR”/“Kyra/KLR marketing”) are used for sales/price and inventory decision support. Weather tools are consulted ad hoc; a formal grass budget tool is not yet embedded. Do you currently have a detailed farm map including paddock mapping? Yes Notes: Yes. Paddock mapping is…

engagements.body: AgriProve Project Proposal Playbook Please list all operators full names, emails, phone numbers Notes: Name: Richard Cox Phone: 0409721830 Email: richard@cracowstation.com Name: Sarah Kate Cox Phone: 0418 152 859 Email: sarah@cracowstation.com Land Titles: 11/DW215 23/DW516 Please list all landowners full names, emails, phone numbers Notes: Name: Richard Cox Phone: 0409721830 Email: richard@cracowstation.com Please provide a brief history of your farm Krakow Station has been in Sarah’s family for approximately a century (“in my wife’s family … for 123 years”). Richard and Sarah assumed ownership and day-to-day management roughly twenty-two years ago (around 2004). The enterprise has always been grazing. Historically the station functioned as a 600 head breeder block, with cattle transferred to other properties. Over the past two decades the managers have focused on rebuilding the herd, improving water security and paddock layout, and progressively investing in infrastructure to support planned grazing. A smaller block that was resumed for mining in the 1960s was bought back by the family ~15 years ago and is now managed with the rest of the holding .Cracow Station has been in the family for 122 years. Always been grazing operation. Richard and Sarah have also implemented an 8 year Cap X program. Please provide a brief description of your background, any relevant accreditations, skills and experience and any ongoing training that assist in managing the land: [Please include any current agronomic advice] Richard was born on a cattle station in West Africa. Richard’s background is in pastoral operations. He completed station training and worked across northern Australia, including stock and management roles (e.g. Stanbroke) and a period in the United States with a diversified ranch family, gaining exposure to multiple on-farm enterprises. He is active in producer networks and research/producer representation (e.g., “producer rep on the managing … committee” noted), and is engaged with grazing education such as RCS/Andrews-style rehydration (natural sequence) concepts. Richard emphasizes stockmanship and dog handling, noting animal calmness and weight gain as key levers. Also completed the Stuart Andrews course. The business runs to a written, staged, eight-year capital works plan to spread risk across seasons while incrementally improving pastures, fencing, water and grazing control. No specific agronomist of record was named in the call; fertilizer and lime are not currently applied in the project area. Please provide a summary of your soil carbon project philosophy and goals: Richard's soil carbon project philosophy and goals treats soil carbon as a long-term measurement and feedback tool aligned with production. The philosophy is to improve soil structure, water distribution and retention, biological function and groundcover through planned grazing, legume establishment and landscape rehydration. Monitoring over time is intended to validate that capital investments and management changes are improving both productivity and soil condition. Do you use any farm management software or digital tools? Or do you have any plans to implement any additional solutions to assist with record keeping? What do you currently use for monitoring and record keeping? At the moment, Phoenix is used for mapping and accounting. Stock numbers and drafting/weighing are handled with Gallagher hardware plus spreadsheets. The business continuously evaluates software options but has not yet found a perfect fit; upgrades are being considered as grazing control increases. Do you use any predictive modelling to assist in management decisions? Yes—Richard KLR Marketing tools (referred to as “KLR”/“Kyra/KLR marketing”) are used for sales/price and inventory decision support. Weather tools are consulted ad hoc; a formal grass budget tool is not yet embedded. Do you currently have a detailed farm map including paddock mapping? Yes Notes: Yes. Paddock mapping is…

engagements.subject: Rene Stud - Your HORIZON Snapshot is ready
engagements.body: Hi Scott, Thanks for your time recently hosting Hobbs at your property in Culcairn. We've run Rene Stud through our HORIZON platform and the results are worth talking about. Click here to view the link to your HORIZON snapshot report: https://canva.link/gcin0wjblc6s9wt. It's also attached in this email for your review. We've established that 889 hectares of your property came back eligible. That's 83.6% of your total area, and for a grazing operation in the Culcairn district, that's a strong result. The soil profile across your paddocks tells a good story too. Depth is a standout, with the majority of your country returning profiles above a metre, and your central-eastern paddocks and eastern boundary are lighting up as your strongest-performing ground. There's also real upside sitting in your western and southern country, where the HORIZON model is pointing to meaningful carbon-building potential under good grazing management. What that translates to is an estimated 66,683 ACCUs over a 25-year crediting period. That's a carbon asset built on country you're already running, through the management you're already doing. We've put together a HORIZON Snapshot for Rene Stud that steps through exactly what we found, how the numbers stack up, and what the project would look like in practice. AgriProve has active projects running in your district. The country around Culcairn is proving itself, and Rene Stud fits the profile well. We'd love the chance to walk you through it properly. If you've got 20 minutes in the next week or two, I'm confident you'll find it worthwhile. I have availability this week and next. Does a call suit you? engagements.subject: Re: Rene Stud - Your HORIZON Snapshot is ready
engagements.body: Hi Scott, Thanks again for the chat yesterday. Looking ahead to next steps for your Land Management Strategy and Project Design Call in a week or two. engagements.subject: Follow up from Friday's conversation
engagements.body: Hi Mark, Thanks again for the chat last Friday. I just wanted to response to you based off your questions regarding AgriProve remains at the forefront of Australia’s soil carbon industry, having delivered the country’s first soil carbon credits, pioneered digital MRV systems and registered over 600 projects nationwide with more than 120,000 Australian Carbon Credit Units issued to date. We have invested 25 million dollars into satellite monitoring and carbon forecasting algorithms to addressable Australian Carbon market. AgriProve was named AFR Sustainability Leaders Winner in Agriculture and Environment Recognising Innovative Technology last year. that Delivers Rapid Results and have recently received an $11.5 million dollar grant. AgriProve has successfully completed the $11.55 million National Soil Carbon Innovation Challenge (NSCIC) grant, finalising development of its groundbreaking Soil Organic Carbon (SOC) model in partnership with EOS Data Analytics. Built using over 20,000 physical soil samples and more than 300 predictors, the model combines multi-band SAR and optical data through a Random Forest ensemble machine learning approach to accurately estimate SOC stocks across Australia’s diverse landscapes. Once your project is registered, you will have access to the SOC model in the next 2-3 months to calibrate the monthly level which will effectively analyze your carbon stocks. The company continues to work closely with industry, government and scientific partners to expand participation and strengthen Australia’s position as a global leader in carbon removal through agriculture, so we plan on being here for a very long time. As far as the 25 year longevity of the project, AgriProve will conduct a 5 year project review to access the viability of the project. This is a anniversary review of the declaration of your project and the opportunity to review performance. If no increases have occurred you have the right to delist the project with no obligations or costs to you as the landholder.
