engagements.subject: RE: Re: AgriProve Soil Carbon Project Next Steps
engagements.body: Hi Mark and Amanda, Following on from our visit and checking in with the severe weather that is occurring in your region. Have you had any further questions regarding project design, mapping or registration intent following on from our conversation a fortnight ago? From my notes, the topics we discussed were: Core Concern: Project Design & Configuration Your primary concern was whether work done in certain areas (specifically high country) would materially increase the baseline or disadvantage them. We have addressed this by configuring the project by isolating the high country into a specific project, demonstrating the design was built with their best interests in mind while maximising usability. We will work with you to register projects as you want – we can align this to implementation, baselining or ability for success. It may be that we register the two highest potential projects in the near term, and then look to work out how best to maximise the leucaena country that is more advanced in the carbon and farm improvement approach. Key Context You want to set this project up in line with family succession planning, with your overriding priority is setting it up for long-term success and maximising carbon credit (ACCU) potential. Project Proponent Discussion Your lawyers had advised you to act as project proponent to maintain control of ACCUs. We will set up an ANREU account that your entitlement of ACCUs produced will be transferred to you within 10-business days of being issued, you will have full control for your share of ACCUs. As we discussed, I clarified the additional regulatory and compliance responsibilities that come with that role, and why having those obligations managed externally gives the project the best chance of compliance and success. Implementation / Grazing Management You intend to make grazing management changes but are not interested in intensive cell grazing — you want a more holistic, flexible approach. you want someone on-site to assess what changes are realistic and where the opportunities lie. We can provide you with a video call with our Grazier in Residence (Hobbs Magaret); he will happily provide you with some tangible practice changes that can align to your overall philosophy. We will not likely be able to have Hobbs come to farm, as he is based in Albury. Baseline & Costs Baseline sampling costs were discussed. The upfront cost is not insignificant, but the framing was that carbon income is supplementary — cream on top of the farming enterprise. As mentioned, the baseline costs will be as quoted in the KCT that you have received and is inclusive of all projects, we invoice this on a project by project basis, so there may be a phased costing approach for the baseline sampling, depending on when this occurs. We are also flexible if you choose to split some between upfront payment and future ACCUs (if in the event no ACCUs are generated, this amount is payable at 5-years as per the $ amount (not the ACCU number multiplied by spot price); or on project termination prior to projects being awarded ACCUs.). @Mark – please send through the list of questions that you had, that you raised in the meeting. I will endeavour to respond to these questions as quickly as possible. Trevor (decision-maker on farm operations) is the one running the day-to-day grazing program; Shelley is doing the questionnaire + admin work on his behalf. They will invite Trevor to comment on the answers before finalising. Trevor is firmly set in his ways — Ben's view is they're unlikely to pick "new" practices, more likely to apply slight tweaks to existing ones (which still counts as material difference for the method). Property is actively under development — fence + road work happening every week (for rotational grazing + paddock corrections + easier access). Shelley raised this as a concern re: how a changing landscape affects baseline / mapping. Crops + pasture: currently growing oats + barley to compete with wheat; slowly transitioning to pasture mix (~5% achieved). Plan is pasture mix for 10-15 year repeat-growing window. Cattle = commercial; Trevor wants to start a bull program and eventually create their own brand (but understands that's a high-ticket pipe dream unless they build it carefully). Fertiliser: all synthetic; she's pulled the invoice for the entire year and can derive the full historic fertiliser picture from the average cost. Discussed the eligible-activities framing — 2 practices to pick from the 11. Could be fertiliser, pasture rejuvenation, rotational grazing; either new OR a material tweak to existing. Mentions a third party (also farms, writes books, does farm visits, knows US farming context) who Trevor would want to consult — Shelley asked Ben if this person could attend a future farm visit; Ben confirmed open to that. Approach agreed: Shelley sends the sales memo + her offline answers as a document; Ben feeds it through the AI; gap-fill conversation after that to handle anything missing. Saves doing the full LMS call again. Then Trevor reviews + comments before final sign-off. Sentiment: Interested / engaged . engagements.body: Hi Alec, Good chat this morning — glad we got into it properly. You made some really valid points, and I want to make sure you've both got something solid to work from before we get on that call Thursday. There's one thing that underpins all of this, and it's what makes the rest pretty straightforward. AgriProve is the one registered with the Clean Energy Regulator with AgriProve as the proponent, the project does not need to be terminated when a farm is sold. AgriProve will work to ensure the project is novated to the new owner, allowing it to continue seamlessly. Click here for link to AgriProve’s role as project proponent Click here for link to The AgriProve Contract - everything your solicitor needs this is provided in the Key Commercial Terms e-document as well. Below are the options there after. So, as a brief explainer if you sell Mallee Park, the person buying it has three options: 1. They want to continue the project. We novate the agreement across to them, they step in, and they inherit a fully running project. For the right buyer that's a genuine asset — it's all set up, they're walking straight into it. 2. They don't want to continue. This is the one that matters most based on what you told me this morning. They don't have to take it on — full stop. AgriProve manages the project administratively, we sample every five years at our own cost, and we carry the risk. No new credits are generated but every ACCU already issued up to the point of sale stays with you. The incoming buyer has no obligation and no exposure. None. 3. The sale happens before credits have been issued. Clean deregistration, no cost, no permanence obligations. We will cover this in more detail next week with our Head of Operations, Will Frecheville on the call — he's the one who actually deals with the CER and handles these situations for over 650 projects that are with AgriProve so a great guy to have on the call. engagements.body: Thanks again George, Looking forward to confirming our 45 minute Land Management Strategy Call with you on Monday the 25th of May at 2pm. In the meantime to proceed to next steps, there are three things that will help us hit the ground running: Eligible Activities A soil carbon project is built around the land management practices you implement on your property — you'll need to adopt at least two, as long as it's genuinely new or materially different from what you've been doing over the past five years. These let us accurately configure your project areas before the call. Five-year farm management history: https://ap1.hubs.ly/y0HwWH0 — this is one of the most important pieces of the puzzle. To accurately model your soil carbon baseline and project what your land can sequester, we need a clear picture of how your properties have been managed over the past five years. Think stocking rates, pasture management, any significant land use changes — the more detail the better. Don't worry if it's not perfectly documented; we'll work through it together on the call. AgriProve Project Proposal Playbook Please list all operators full names, emails, phone numbers Notes: Name: Edward Ohlrich Email: edward.ohlrich@gmail.com Phone: 0402947648 Name: Rodney Perrett Email: rodneyperrett@iinet.net.au Phone: 07 4984 4527 Land Titles: 90/SP276282 1/SP333857 137/CH311562 Please list all landowners full names, emails, phone numbers Notes: Name: Edward Ohlrich Email: edward.ohlrich@gmail.com Phone: 0402947648 Name: Rodney Perrett Email: rodneyperrett@iinet.net.au Phone: (07) 4984 4527 Please provide a brief history of your farm Edward and his business partner acquired the "Mount Moon" property in June 2022. Since acquisition, they have bought and sold steeper, more forested country and now hold a larger area than appears in the land-title records referenced on the call, with a view to focusing on country that is better suited to a soil carbon project. Historically, the land formed part of a larger enterprise called “Kingpah” (spelling as given on the call), which operated as a trading and fattening enterprise with larger paddocks. Prior to Edward’s ownership there was a period under another owner who invested in new fencing and water and created smaller paddock sizes that better suit rotational grazing. Edward has continued with that rotational approach. Acquired the property in June 2022. Please provide a brief description of your background, any relevant accreditations, skills and experience and any ongoing training that assist in managing the land: [Please include any current agronomic advice] Edward is a periodontist with substantial business ownership experience and intermittent agricultural involvement throughout his life. He has been actively involved in agriculture for the past three years. He is currently enrolled in the RCS “Next Steps” program focused on grazing training. Business partner has involved in agriculture for 80 years. Please provide a summary of your soil carbon project philosophy and goals: At Mount Moon Pastoral, Edward’s approach to the carbon project is grounded in the understanding that productive grazing and soil carbon sequestration can—and should—work hand in hand. The project will focus on creating optimal conditions for both, recognising that improvements in one area will reinforce gains in the other through a positive feedback loop. This will involve a range of eligible activities that enhance soil biology. The overarching goal is to enhance soil structure, water retention, and ecological function, ultimately leading to healthier soils, higher carbon levels, and increased pasture productivity. By committing to a long-term soil carbon project, Mount Moon Pastoral will gain access to ongoing monitoring and data-driven insights into land management practices. This feedback loop will help guide continual improvement—delivering benefits not only in carbon outcomes but also in the resilience and profitability of the grazing enterprise. Do you use any farm management software or digital tools? Or do you have any plans to implement any additional solutions to assist with record keeping? What do you currently use for monitoring and record keeping? Edward records operational information in an app he referred to on the call as Mobble and uses it particularly for livestock weights and treatments. He also uses an Datamars for recording items related to livestock weights and treatments. Do you use any predictive modelling to assist in management decisions? Yes. Edward uses Excel spreadsheets provided through RCS on a subscription basis to support grazing and financial planning decisions. Do you currently have a detailed farm map including paddock mapping? Yes Are you aware of any land clearing occurring: a.) In the past 7 years (if there has been no change in title ownership)? b.) In the past 5 years (if there has been change in title ownership )? No If land clearing has occurred please describe where, when, and how, noting the land titles that the activity occurred across. No. Edwar…

Follow up from last week meeting
engagements.body: Hi Edward, Thanks again for your time last week with Will and I last week, I hope it was helpful as we look to finalize signing off to your Carbon Project Plan. I promised I would send you a follow up in relation to: Having your own account set up for generating ACCU's once we have registered the project. A simplified rationale around sale of farm and ACCU's We will be moving to a more regular position where all of our landholders and partners will be required to have their own ANREU account to hold their ACCUs Setting up an ANREU account can be done via the CER's website; or we can do it on behalf of the landholder once your Key Commercial Terms have bene signed. https://cer.gov.au/online-systems/anreu-account-guidance: https://cer.gov.au/online-systems/anreu-account-guidance What this means, is we have a number of marking positives and offerings that can be put to you, the landholder: We can absolutely set up an ANREU account for you Landholder has full flexibility and autonomy of their ACCUs You can elect to sell either through AgriProve or on their own, or through another broker This avoids a brokerage fee or holding fee from AgriProve if they have their ACCUs transferred and broker through someone else. The accounts are assessed by a separate team, so will not have any impact on any assessments for their carbon project. In addition, I want to address something that you brought up on sale of farm and ACCU's - what happens if circumstances change down the track? We've designed your project to be flexible and future-proof. After your initial baseline soil sampling, AgriProve carries all ongoing project costs for the 25-year lifespan. This means: ✓ You can focus your carbon-building efforts on the areas showing best results ✓ If you sell the property, the project transfers smoothly to the new owner ✓ You're not locked into something that could become a liability Why AgriProve Being the "Proponent" Matters to You: In simple terms - AgriProve take on the project responsibility. With AgriProve as proponent, we're responsible for transferring the project to the new landholder. They're actually inheriting something valuable - you've already paid for the baseline sampling, and AgriProve covers all future costs. It makes the project very attractive for them to continue. AgriProve as Proponent - How We Protect You: https://help.agriprove.io/faq-agriprove-as-proponent-what-are-the-benefits Your Safety Valve - The 5-Year Review: We're not locking you into something that doesn't perform. At the 5-year mark, we review the project together. If you haven't seen the carbon increases we projected, you can walk away - no obligations, no costs, no penalties. It's our way of ensuring we deliver what we promise. What If the New Owner Says No? Two straightforward options: Option 1 - Dormancy (Most Common): The project goes dormant. AgriProve maintains the Clean Energy Regulator obligations and covers all costs. The new landholder doesn't have to actively participate - we just keep it ticking over. No impact on you. Option 2 - Termination (Rare): If termination happens completely outside our control, ACCUs would need to be returned to the regulator. But here's the key: AgriProve carries the risk of ACCU relinquishment unless you terminate the project in breach of our agreement. This is additional protection for you. Bottom Line: You're not taking on a 25-year liability that could bite you if life changes. We've structured this so you can: Generate potential carbon revenue with confidence Sell your property without complications Exit at 5 years if results aren't there Have AgriProve carry the long-term risk Future Visibility - Real-Time Carbon Tracking: Lastly, within 2-3 months, you'll have access to our Soil Organic Carbon (SOC) model in Horizon: https://agriprove.io/in-the-news-old/mr-wsd-horizon-launch. Think of it as a monthly health check on your carbon stocks - you'll know exactly where you stand, no surprises. If you have any feedback or fu…

engagements.subject: Your AgriProve HORIZON Snapshot – S and G Duncan
engagements.body: Hi Steven, Thanks for your interest in exploring soil carbon at your Bullcamp property. I've attached your HORIZON Snapshot, which shows the estimated opportunity based on our analysis across both of your land parcels. You have 233 eligible hectares, with Sodosol soils that — under your 844mm annual rainfall — create conditions suited to carbon accumulation. The analysis shows Strength Zones through the central and southern sections of the western paddocks and across the middle of the northeastern block, where modelled carbon levels currently sit above the property median. Opportunity Zones across the northern and western portions of both parcels indicate where management adjustments could support meaningful gains. With soil depths reaching 1.70m, there's solid capacity for carbon storage in the profile. We're projecting approximately 23,329 ACCUs over 25 years based on your rainfall band — a genuine volume for a property of this scale. The eligible area shown is derived from automated satellite analysis and should be treated as a reference. Our geospatial team conducts a detailed property assessment as part of the next stage, combining expert interpretation with your on-ground knowledge. If you notice managed land that appears to have been excluded, our team will work together with you to review and, where appropriate, include it in your project area. There is one important consideration to share openly: our registered projects are typically structured around a minimum of 400 eligible hectares, where the economics work most effectively for landholders. At 233 ha, your property would need to be paired with a neighbouring property to form a viable registered project. This is a well-travelled path — aggregated projects are common in the South Burnett region — and it's something I'd love to explore with you if you have neighbours who might be interested. In the meantime, the HORIZON analysis gives you a clear picture of where carbon potential sits across your property and where focused management could build on the existing Strength Zones. I'd be happy to jump on a call to talk through the maps in more detail, I'll give you a call this week. engagements.body: Hi Daniel, I hope you are well. Just wanted to cover some of the final points with the Carbon Project Plan for Calca Block. My operation officer has just asked a few questions so we can get this issued to you: Please see below: Propose merging projects 1 and 2 on scrub country to allow for flexibility with paddock alterations and new fenceline positioning. This combined area can be registered as a single Carbon Estimation Area and subdivided into a number of strata so that we have adequate sampling density. This will simplify things in terms of record keeping and emissions accounting. See revised Project Area Confirmation map. Is fertiliser usage limited to the southern cropped areas only? Confirm whether any grazing areas have fertiliser applied. This eligible activity would then only apply to projects 2 & 3 (based on new config). Provide detail of cropping system management. If we can get Daniel to complete the table on page 11 of the attached Project Proposal doc. Provide detail on grazing practice over the cropped country? For how long on average and is it the whole mob? i.e. summer grazing of stubbles every year/second year, ~2,000 sheep for 3 months, dependent on available feed etc. For the information on grazing management in the playbook, does the 783 ha refer to the cropped areas of projects 2 and 3 to the south? Then 1,400 ha refer to the scrub pasture areas to the north? Have tillage passes in the baseline period been done strictly on the cropped areas? What is done on the scrub areas to the south in and around the cropped areas? Are sheep allowed to graze unrestricted on these areas when they are grazing stubbles? Based on satellite images and our knowledge of the region, presence of limestone/rock outcrops should be excluded from the project area. It would be good to gain further understanding of what the southern scrub areas are like in terms of rock/compaction and sampling ability and whether larger areas need to be excluded from the project. engagements.subject: Your Key Commercial Terms - Important update from AgriProve
engagements.body: Hi Daniel, I hope the start of the has been treating you well. I'm reaching out because we've made some significant changes to AgriProve's Key Commercial Terms based on direct feedback from farmers like yourself. Your previous terms document has been paused while we bring everyone across to the new framework. The short version: we've listened to what producers have told us wasn't working, and we've fixed it. What's changed? • Your ACCUs, your account - We'll help you set up your own ANREU account. Once credits are generated, they sit with you, not us. You decide when and how to trade them. • Complete transparency on the 75/25 split - No more ambiguity. Your entitlement is explicitly calculated: total ACCUs × 75%, minus any owed for additional services. Simple maths, clear outcomes. • Exit pathway if numbers don't work - After baseline sampling (before year 5 reporting), we review results together. If the project doesn't stack up commercially, you can walk away with no further obligations. • Capped financial exposure - Clear 5-year limit on what you'd owe if ACCU generation doesn't cover baseline costs. No surprises down the track. • We're more accountable than ever before - If AgriProve doesn't deliver, you have defined pathways to replace us or exit entirely, with proper transition support. These changes are designed to remove that complexity. engagements.subject: Follow up for our call this week— the key points
engagements.body: Hi Geoff, Thanks again for the call this week. I just wanted to come back to you on the key points you raised over the phone this week. 1. Rainfall and sequestration viability you mentioned that you have been told by others that soil carbon is "wholly and solely reliant on rainfall" and is potentially sceptical about whether drier conditions stack up. Our position is that rainfall is a necessary condition for carbon sequestration, but it does not cause carbon sequestration. We have seen projects with high rainfall that have not resulted in sequestration and have seen low rainfall projects be awarded credits. It is our belief and observations from our portfolio that management, that is how you capture, use and manage the water on your land is a critical aspect to carbon sequestration. 2. Carbon credits and carbon neutrality claims You have heard at a meeting (possibly a Riverina co-op event) that selling ACCUs means losing carbon neutrality status, and that one farmer had to buy credits back at a premium to restore their neutral balance. This is not necessarily true. A claim of carbon neutrality can be made when the emissions from a property are neutralised via sequestration or offsets. Claiming carbon neutrality and participating in a carbon project are two independent programs. Each requires their own audits and assessments if a verifiable claim is to be made. In determining whether a business is carbon neutral, all emissions sources are accounted for (e.g. livestock, fertiliser, lime, fuel, electricity, etc) and then checked against any sequestration (trees and soil). If there is a deficit, where total emissions exceed total sequestration, then to claim carbon neutrality you must source an eligible offsets unit and retire that unit to be able to claim carbon neutrality (i.e. offsetting emissions). An ACCU is one of a number of eligible offsets units, so it can be ‘retired’ to support this claim. If there is a surplus of sequestration, (i.e. carbon stores from trees or soil is greater than emissions) then there is no need to purchase offsets to claim carbon neutrality. Additionally, in this scenario, any credits that have been generated above that carbon neutral amount, can be sold, and the claim can still be made that you are carbon neutral. Where this messaging in industry becomes murky is that if you sell all ACCUs (that have been generated via soil or tree sequestration) then this sequestration cannot be measured against the emissions to claim carbon neutrality. The claim that you can’t sell ACCUs and claim carbon neutrality is based on the assumption that sequestration will not exceed emissions and there will be no surplus ACCUs to be able to sell. This is not correct. The key determinant in claiming carbon neutrality is that the emissions have been neutralised either via sequestration and/or offsets. If you generate ACCUs through participating in a soil carbon or ACCU scheme project and hold them in your ANREU account, you have the flexibility to sell, retain/hold or retire the ACCUs depending on your needs and priorities, and the yearly carbon emissions assessment. If you do not have an ANREU account, you cannot hold ACCUs to offset against your emissions, you must source these eligible credits units by purchasing on a secondary market. In partnering with AgriProve and participating in a soil carbon project, you will be set up with your own ANREU account, and that 75% of the ACCUs awarded to the project will be held in your own ANREU account to use in the manner that you have deemed best for your business. 3. ACCU pricing and the "premium" question You'd heard $68/ACCU on ABC News and was trying to make sense of it against spot ($37.50 at call time). You're across the basic answer now (broker-facilitated premiums for high-integrity credits with a good story), but it's natural to be thinking hard about whether the economics stack up and what his exit options look like at different price points. engagements.body: Hi Tom and Rachel, Thank you both for taking the time to speak with me last while on the road to Sydney. I really appreciated the opportunity to learn more about your operations and discuss how AgriProve's: https://agriprove.io/ soil carbon program might align with your farm management practices. Based on our discussion, I wanted to confirm a few important aspects of how AgriProve's program works: What We Do (and Don't Do): We focus exclusively on soil carbon sequestration - no tree planting or land lock-up requirements You retain complete control over your farming decisions and land management We don't dictate agronomic practices or align with specific agronomists/products The program is farmer-led - you continue managing your properties as you see fit Your Properties: Your three properties totaling 4,000 hectares meet our criteria well. We typically work with properties above 300-400 hectares, and your average rainfall of 880mm is excellent for soil carbon projects (we've had success with rainfall as low as 340mm/year). Financial Structure: No upfront costs until baseline soil sampling We cover all ongoing costs: administration, registration, monitoring, mapping, and audits 75/25 split: You receive 75% of carbon credits (ACCUs), we receive 25% to cover all project costs We only get paid when you get paid - aligning our interests with yours. Project Flexibility: 25-year project term with a 5-year review point where you can assess progress and decide whether to continue If sequestration isn't occurring as expected, there's an exit pathway No penalties for carbon loss due to drought, fire, or other uncontrollable events - you simply resume earning credits from your highest watermark Multiple properties can be enrolled separately, so you receive credits as soon as the first property shows measurable increases Addressing Your Specific Concerns: Given Rachel's 38 years of agronomic experience and your long-term focus on rotational grazing and soil improvement, I understand your carbon levels may already be relatively high. This is where our Horizon: https://agriprove.io/in-the-news-old/mr-wsd-horizon-launch technology becomes valuable - it provides a desktop assessment of your specific soil carbon potential based on your property's characteristics, soil types, pH, and organic matter levels. Regarding your excellent work with lime application to address soil acidity (pH 4.3-4.4), this could potentially qualify as a materially different practice under the program if you're increasing application rates or expanding coverage areas. The key is that practices must be either: Brand new to the property, or Materially different from what you've done in the previous 7 years (e.g., increased application rates, different timing, expanded areas) Your rotational grazing practices over the past 50 years demonstrate strong land stewardship. Unlike previous consultants, we would never recommend fencing off your upland wetland or changing management approaches that are working well for you. Your use of livestock behavior as an indicator of paddock health is exactly the type of informed management that makes soil carbon projects successful. Property Transfer Question: If you sell a property during the project term, AgriProve acts as the project proponent and maintains responsibility for project continuity. We can discuss transfer options with potential buyers, or you can choose to exit the project according to the terms and conditions. AgriProve Project Proposal Playbook Please list all operators full names, emails, phone numbers Notes: Matthew O'Neil (Father of Adam) Ph: 0428 112 319 email: matthew_oneill1@bigpond.com Angus O'Neil - Ph: 0484615124 email: angusoneill110@gmail.com Please list all landowners full names, emails, phone numbers Notes: Angus O'Neil - Ph: 0484615124 email: angusoneill110@gmail.com Please provide a brief history of your farm Angus O'Neil's farm is know as Berrima which is situated in Mendooran, NSW 115 Castlereagh Highway. The property was purchased in 1954 and has been in the family for three generations. The property sits at 405 h/a which has recently been split into two parts. Traditionally been a mixed cropping operation originally. The last 25 years has seen very minimum inputs have gone into the property. Over a 25 years period, grandparents of Angus have run with the practice of a low stocking rate, nature pastures, very little super applied history and the occasional Oat crop with synthetic fertilizers. In the last four year, Father Matthew (father to Angus) took the farm over and leased off the parents then started doubling cropping, increasing the fertilizer program and introducing legumes into cropping. As of last month the property was transferred to Angus O'Neil, son of Matthew O'Neil Please provide a brief description of your background, any relevant accreditations, skills and experience and any ongoing training that assist in managing the land: [Please include any current agronomic advice] Angus owner/manager along with manager and father Matthew O'Neil both grew up on farm. Matthew (father) has managed grazing properties throughout his career. Both Matthew and Angus moved back to the Mendooran property 4-5 years ago where they leased the property from the grandparents. Angus attended UNE and undertook a double bachelor in Bachelor of Agriculture and Bachelor of Agriculture Business with a minor in Agronomy. Since then, Angus has been working on grazing properties over the last five years. Additionally, Angus used to live and worked with a landowner that run a regenerative and organic farm in Armidale NSW which Angus obtained a certificate as part of the time he spend on the Armidale property. Please provide a summary of your soil carbon project philosophy and goals: The goal for Angus and the property is approaching a soil carbon project knowing the property hasn't run to it's fullest potential. Firstly, based on a soil carbon project, Angus wants to maximize the farms production economically and in doing so he realizes that he has to also maximize the carbon sequestration and the health of the soils overall. The philosophy over the duration of the project is to not only improve the productivity through further sequestration of carbon, but have the ability to monitor and understand where they are currently at with the practices he has started to implement. These include increasing legumes in pasture rotation and summer cropping rotation, double cropping and the plan to implement bio solids space in an attempt to step away from synthetic fertilizers in pasture rotation. Angus would also like to validate that the practices whether they be new or materially different are going to be suited to sequester further carbon from the soil through continued implementation and monitoring of farm management. Do you use any farm management software or digital tools? Or do you have any plans to implement any additional solutions to assist with record keeping? What do you currently use for monitoring and record keeping? Currently uses traditional methods of hard copy note books and calendars on phones. Angus is looking at using looking Agriwebb in the near future to keep track of cattle number and ESI on sheep from a productional and operational perspective. engagements.body: Hi Angus, Thanks again for the chat last week. The reason for this email is to ensure I'm answering the questions you had about the potential sale of the farm and ACCU's sold or earnt on the same project area. These are very common questions and I'll ensure transparency is the top priority here as always. Firstly, AgriProve has carefully designed your project to stay within enterprise types and land titles while onboarding all associated costs for the lifespan of the project, after the initial bassline soil sampling. This future proofs for sale of land and drastically increases sampling flexibility, allowing you to earn ACCUs in the areas your focusing improvement efforts on. As AgriProve is the proponent to the project, we shoulder the responsibility to ensure the incoming landholder (if property has been sold) wants to take over the project. Below is a link that explains the benefits of AgriProve's part as proponent to the project (please read the link to understand how we play the role as proponent carefully) AgriProve as proponent: https://help.agriprove.io/faq-agriprove-as-proponent-what-are-the-benefits Essentially, if AgriProve weren't the proponent to the project and the incoming landholder didn't want to continue on with the project, then you (the outgoing landholder) would be left needing to pay all the credits you've generated to the regulator because you haven't fulfilled the 25 year project. With AgriProve as proponent, we are responsible to novate that agreement across from current project owner to incoming landowner. They inherit to an extent a free project as you've already covered cost of initial baseline and AgriProve covers the costs for the remaining lifespan of the project which makes it extremely attractive to carry on with implementing practices. Keep in mind with your registered carbon project, AgriProve will conduct a 5 year project review to access the viability of the project. This is a anniversary review of the declaration of your project and the opportunity to review performance. If no increases have occurred you have the right to delist the project with no obligations or costs to the landholder. AgriProve will also have a SOC model live (Soil Organic Carbon) within the next 2-3 months that your project will have access to so you know where your carbon stocks are at with the intention to review your carbon stock levels on a monthly basis. If they don't want to inherit the project, there are a few options... Dormacy. AgriProve incur the costs to maintain the obligation to the Clen Energy Regulator of upholding the project. The new landholders don't have to actively take part in the project, it will just go dormant and AgriProve have to incur the costs of keeping the project ticking over. Termination If there is a termination of the project that is totally outside of AgriProve's control, essentially you would have to return the entire amount of project ACCU's delivered by the CER (Clen Energy Regulator) to the project. Who is responsible for ACCU relinquishment if the project ends prematurely? AgriProve takes on the risk of ACCU relinquishment unless the project is terminated by the landholder in breach of our Master Terms and Conditions: https://ap1.hubs.ly/y0nl_30, such as within the 25-year permanence period. This provides additional protection for the landholder. engagements.body: Thanks again for the chat this week. As mentioned, we are looking at simplifying by moving to a more regular position where all of our landholders and partners will be required to have their own ANREU account to hold their ACCUs. Setting up an ANREU account can be done via the CER's (Clean Energy Regulator) website; or we can do it on behalf of the landholder once your Key Commercial Terms have bene signed. https://cer.gov.au/online-systems/anreu-account-guidance: https://cer.gov.au/online-systems/anreu-account-guidance What this means, is we have a number of marking positives and offerings that can be put to the landholder. We can absolutely set up an ANREU account for you Landholder has full flexibility and autonomy of their ACCUs You can elect to sell either through AgriProve or on their own, or through another broker This avoids a brokerage fee or holding fee from AgriProve if they have their ACCUs transferred and broker through someone else. We will look for formalize a process for setting up these accounts, starting with our landholders who have already been issued credits, and then working through clients with a measured increase and then onto clients as a part of their onboarding/re-sampling. The accounts are assessed by a separate team, so will not have any impact on any assessments for their carbon project. It's worth noting that when you are within the crediting process, AgriProve will reconfirm your intent for ACCU's at the time of crediting to you so there is flexibility. Let me know when you have a chance to send through the questions that you mentioned you had for us. We are also the fastest crediting soil carbon developer in the market. Allan has managed properties in the past and has now spent 20 years on the Hernani property and also attended the majority courses that the Local Land Services on pasture and soils. Please provide a summary of your soil carbon project philosophy and goals: Our soil carbon project philosophy is grounded in the belief that productive agriculture and long-term carbon sequestration are not only compatible but mutually reinforcing. By improving soil health through targeted interventions — such as pH correction, enhanced biodiversity, and adaptive grazing management — we aim to create a regenerative feedback loop where increased pasture productivity supports greater carbon inputs, and enhanced soil function enables deeper, more stable carbon storage. The core goals of the project are to: Build long-term soil carbon stocks through improved management of soil biology, structure, and vegetation. Enhance primary productivity by increasing pasture resilience, water retention, and nutrient availability. Integrate carbon farming with existing operations, ensuring that carbon gains support — rather than compete with — the productivity of cattle enterprises. Generate reliable, measurable outcomes through ongoing soil monitoring and data-driven feedback, enabling continual refinement of land management practices. Deliver environmental and economic value by aligning improved farm performance with access to carbon markets and long-term sustainability outcomes. This approach positions carbon farming not as a separate activity, but as a natural extension of regenerative land management — benefiting both the landholder and the landscape. engagements.body: Hi Georgina, I hope the start of the has been treating you well. I'm reaching out because we've made some significant changes to AgriProve's Key Commercial Terms based on direct feedback from farmers like yourself. engagements.subject: Why Southern Queensland is Australia's carbon capital
engagements.body: G'Day Emma, Ben from AgriProve here. I wanted to personally reach out because you're farming in what is objectively Australia's most productive region for soil carbon projects and I thought you should know why that matters for your bottom line. Let's talk about the Southern Queensland soil profile: Southern Queensland sits in the sweet spot for ideal soil profiles, resulting in soil carbon sequestration. Vertosols, Dermosols and Chromosol soil types can sequester higher than average carbon stocks that translates directly to potential ACCUs (Australian Carbon Credit Units) per hectare. engagements.subject: AgriProve as project proponent
engagements.body: Hi Brenton, I watned to follow up on our discussion about project proponent, as I understand the approach seems different to what producers would initially perceive as the risk adverse option, being proponent themselves. As it isn't intuitively obvious the reasons why landowners as proponent is potentially more risky, I want to take the time to explain the benefits of AgriProve as proponent in writing and stress that this has been done to reduce risk on the producer and increase uptake. AgriProve acting as proponent means we are responsible for regulatory compliance associated legal (civil and criminal) penalties for non-compliance, and reduces the regulatory and compliance risk to the landholder. It also means we are the primary contact point with the CER and allows us to handle these communications with our significant compliance expertise, reducing administrative burden on landowners. AgriProve as proponent affords flexibility of management to the landholder, with the ability to cease the active project implementation at any time. As proponent we then maintain the project administratively and ensure it remains compliant to avoid ACCU relinquishment. These administrative requirements would fall to a landholder as proponent for managing a non-active project. Risk associated with potential ACCU relinquishment requirements are borne by AgriProve where these relinquishment requirements are not due to a breach of our Master Terms and Conditions (such as complete termination of the project my the operator/landowner within the project 25 year permanence period) AgriProve acting as proponent provides a mechanism for sale of farm without terminating projects and requiring ACCUs to be relinquished - the project remains active with AgriProve and we have a vested interest in assisting with project agreement novation to new owners. Efficiency of start-up - we can get registrations lodged immediately. Landowner as proponent would need to get established with the CER before being able to register projects. This could add an additional 3 months to the process. I hope this helps clarify some of our conversation. As always, give be a bell if you have any questions. Speak soon. engagements.body: G'Day Brenton, Ben from AgriProve here. I wanted to personally reach out because, as a business dedicated to working extensively across the Central Queensland Coast, and I thought you might be interested in what we're seeing happen right across the region. engagements.subject: How a Southern Queensland farmer achieved positive results with AgriProve
engagements.body: Brenton, Final time I'll personally reach out (promise). I couldn't miss the opportunity to tell you about another farmer based in the Southern Queensland region doing something pretty remarkable. engagements.subject: AgriProve as project proponent
engagements.body: Hi Brenton, I watned to follow up on our discussion about project proponent, as I understand the approach seems different to what producers would initially perceive as the risk adverse option, being proponent themselves. As it isn't intuitively obvious the reasons why landowners as proponent is potentially more risky, I want to take the time to explain the benefits of AgriProve as proponent in writing and stress that this has been done to reduce risk on the producer and increase uptake. AgriProve acting as proponent means we are responsible for regulatory compliance associated legal (civil and criminal) penalties for non-compliance, and reduces the regulatory and compliance risk to the landholder. It also means we are the primary contact point with the CER and allows us to handle these communications with our significant compliance expertise, reducing administrative burden on landowners. AgriProve as proponent affords flexibility of management to the landholder, with the ability to cease the active project implementation at any time. As proponent we then maintain the project administratively and ensure it remains compliant to avoid ACCU relinquishment. These administrative requirements would fall to a landholder as proponent for managing a non-active project. Risk associated with potential ACCU relinquishment requirements are borne by AgriProve where these relinquishment requirements are not due to a breach of our Master Terms and Conditions (such as complete termination of the project my the operator/landowner within the project 25 year permanence period) AgriProve acting as proponent provides a mechanism for sale of farm without terminating projects and requiring ACCUs to be relinquished - the project remains active with AgriProve and we have a vested interest in assisting with project agreement novation to new owners. Efficiency of start-up - we can get registrations lodged immediately. Landowner as proponent would need to get established with the CER before being able to register projects. This could add an additional 3 months to the process. I hope this helps clarify some of our conversation. As always, give be a bell if you have any questions. Speak soon. engagements.subject: AgriProve as project proponent
engagements.body: Hi Brenton, I watned to follow up on our discussion about project proponent, as I understand the approach seems different to what producers would initially perceive as the risk adverse option, being proponent themselves. As it isn't intuitively obvious the reasons why landowners as proponent is potentially more risky, I want to take the time to explain the benefits of AgriProve as proponent in writing and stress that this has been done to reduce risk on the producer and increase uptake. AgriProve acting as proponent means we are responsible for regulatory compliance associated legal (civil and criminal) penalties for non-compliance, and reduces the regulatory and compliance risk to the landholder. It also means we are the primary contact point with the CER and allows us to handle these communications with our significant compliance expertise, reducing administrative burden on landowners. AgriProve as proponent affords flexibility of management to the landholder, with the ability to cease the active project implementation at any time. As proponent we then maintain the project administratively and ensure it remains compliant to avoid ACCU relinquishment. These administrative requirements would fall to a landholder as proponent for managing a non-active project. Risk associated with potential ACCU relinquishment requirements are borne by AgriProve where these relinquishment requirements are not due to a breach of our Master Terms and Conditions (such as complete termination of the project my the operator/landowner within the project 25 year permanence period) AgriProve acting as proponent provides a mechanism for sale of farm without terminating projects and requiring ACCUs to be relinquished - the project remains active with AgriProve and we have a vested interest in assisting with project agreement novation to new owners. Efficiency of start-up - we can get registrations lodged immediately. Landowner as proponent would need to get established with the CER before being able to register projects. This could add an additional 3 months to the process. I hope this helps clarify some of our conversation. As always, give be a bell if you have any questions. Speak soon. engagements.subject: AgriProve as project proponent
engagements.body: Hi Brenton, I watned to follow up on our discussion about project proponent, as I understand the approach seems different to what producers would initially perceive as the risk adverse option, being proponent themselves. As it isn't intuitively obvious the reasons why landowners as proponent is potentially more risky, I want to take the time to explain the benefits of AgriProve as proponent in writing and stress that this has been done to reduce risk on the producer and increase uptake. AgriProve acting as proponent means we are responsible for regulatory compliance associated legal (civil and criminal) penalties for non-compliance, and reduces the regulatory and compliance risk to the landholder. It also means we are the primary contact point with the CER and allows us to handle these communications with our significant compliance expertise, reducing administrative burden on landowners. AgriProve as proponent affords flexibility of management to the landholder, with the ability to cease the active project implementation at any time. As proponent we then maintain the project administratively and ensure it remains compliant to avoid ACCU relinquishment. These administrative requirements would fall to a landholder as proponent for managing a non-active project. Risk associated with potential ACCU relinquishment requirements are borne by AgriProve where these relinquishment requirements are not due to a breach of our Master Terms and Conditions (such as complete termination of the project my the operator/landowner within the project 25 year permanence period) AgriProve acting as proponent provides a mechanism for sale of farm without terminating projects and requiring ACCUs to be relinquished - the project remains active with AgriProve and we have a vested interest in assisting with project agreement novation to new owners. Efficiency of start-up - we can get registrations lodged immediately. Landowner as proponent would need to get established with the CER before being able to register projects. This could add an additional 3 months to the process. I hope this helps clarify some of our conversation. As always, give be a bell if you have any questions. Speak soon. engagements.subject: AgriProve as project proponent
engagements.body: Hi Brenton, I watned to follow up on our discussion about project proponent, as I understand the approach seems different to what producers would initially perceive as the risk adverse option, being proponent themselves. As it isn't intuitively obvious the reasons why landowners as proponent is potentially more risky, I want to take the time to explain the benefits of AgriProve as proponent in writing and stress that this has been done to reduce risk on the producer and increase uptake. AgriProve acting as proponent means we are responsible for regulatory compliance associated legal (civil and criminal) penalties for non-compliance, and reduces the regulatory and compliance risk to the landholder. It also means we are the primary contact point with the CER and allows us to handle these communications with our significant compliance expertise, reducing administrative burden on landowners. AgriProve as proponent affords flexibility of management to the landholder, with the ability to cease the active project implementation at any time. As proponent we then maintain the project administratively and ensure it remains compliant to avoid ACCU relinquishment. These administrative requirements would fall to a landholder as proponent for managing a non-active project. Risk associated with potential ACCU relinquishment requirements are borne by AgriProve where these relinquishment requirements are not due to a breach of our Master Terms and Conditions (such as complete termination of the project my the operator/landowner within the project 25 year permanence period) AgriProve acting as proponent provides a mechanism for sale of farm without terminating projects and requiring ACCUs to be relinquished - the project remains active with AgriProve and we have a vested interest in assisting with project agreement novation to new owners. Efficiency of start-up - we can get registrations lodged immediately. Landowner as proponent would need to get established with the CER before being able to register projects. This could add an additional 3 months to the process. I hope this helps clarify some of our conversation. As always, give be a bell if you have any questions. Speak soon. engagements.subject: Why Central Queensland Coastal region is Australia's carbon capital
engagements.body: G'Day Brenton, Ben from AgriProve here. I wanted to personally reach out because, as a business dedicated to working extensively across the Central Queensland Coast, and I thought you might be interested in what we're seeing happen right across the region. Let's talk about the Central Queensland Coast soil profile: Central Queensland Coast is one of the most underrated soil carbon opportunities in Australia. With diverse soil types including Dermosols, Vertosols and Sodosol spanning from the coastal strip right through to the inland brigalow country, this translates directly to potential ACCUs (Australian Carbon Credit Units) per hectare. engagements.subject: How a Southern Queensland farmer achieved positive results with AgriProve
engagements.body: Brenton, Final time I'll personally reach out (promise). I couldn't miss the opportunity to tell you about another farmer based in the Southern Queensland region doing something pretty remarkable. The Smith Carbon Project, located in the Darling Downs, has recently been issued 1,362 Australian Carbon Credit Units (ACCUs) You can read the full case study here: 👉The Smith Carbon Project Case Study: https://agriprove.io/smith-cp-cs1 The project has returned positive carbon sequestration by implementing key practices including: - Multi-species pasture and have increased the diversity of microbial. - Watering points and fencing were installed to support the subdivision of their land into smaller paddocks, increasing rotational grazing intensity.
